a promising approach for tackling complex optimization challenges. A key requirement for RL is the definition of a reward function that guides agent learning. However, designing such functions for optimization remains difficult, often necessitating manual tuning through trial and error, which can deter the broad adoption of RL techniques. We introduce the concept of Rewardless RL, which removes the need for manual reward function design. Instead, the agent relies solely on state-reward-state transitions, allowing it to naturally associate rewards with state qualities rather than specific actions. This framework is particularly valuable in complex optimization scenarios where the target optimal state is unclear, or when combining multiple RL agents into an ensemble requires aligning their individual rewards without disrupting any single agent's incentives. Although the reward function is absent in Rewardless RL, we demonstrate that it can be effectively learned from collected experience using regression techniques. We validate this approach on both synthetic tasks and a real-world multi-armed clustering problem, comparing results against a baseline that utilizes a hand-crafted reward function. In the multi-armed clustering experiment, we further examine how learning a reward function impacts learning speed and algorithm performance. Our findings indicate that Rewardless RL achieves comparable or superior performance to RL with hand-crafted rewards, even when agents are added during training. Additionally, our approach learns a reward function approximately 30% faster than two established methods: inverse reinforcement learning and direct feature weighting. Finally, we open-sour ce our code at https://github.com/ehabry/Rewardless_RL.

Abstract: In this work, we tackle the challenge of recovering a low-rank positive semidefinite (PSD) matrix from a subset of entries. This issue, commonly known as partially observed matrix completion (POMC), arises in various real-world contexts and is generally solved using convex relaxation, specifically semi-definite programming (SDP). While recent heuristic strategies have sought to balance computational efficiency with recovery accuracy, a systematic analysis of how heuristics compare to SDP across different noise levels has been missing. To address this, we develop a differential-equation-based ordinary differential equation (ODE) solver that learns a rank-one PSD matrix from noisy, partially observed data. Our method offers a closed-form formula for the update step, ensuring computational speeds similar to gradient descent while achieving higher recovery accuracy than prior heuristics. Furthermore, we extend this approach to handle rank-k PSD matrices by applying the k-th power of our update step to $k$ carefully selected matrices during optimization. s) typically accrete matter through active galactic nuclei (AGNs), which are categorized into types 1 and 2 based on the presence or absence of obscuring structures like dust and gas. While type 1 AGNs generally exhibit broad emission lines, making their accretion discs observable, type 2 AGNs appear obscured. This study presents the discovery of a rare intermediate case in a type 2 AGN where the dust cone is partially opened, allowing the direct detection of emission from the inner accretion disc. Using the 30-meter-class Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we detected water line emission for the obscured source NGC 4921. Our analysis of this previously unseen water transition reveals a compact source size of approximately 111±34 au at 325 GHz, a scale typical of broad-line region sizes in type 1 AGNs. Applying a modified disc model, we estimated the black hole mass to be between 4.3×10^7 M_sun and 4.7×10^8 M_sun, suggesting that the black hole in NGC 4921 has evolved since 2006. These findings indicate that the obscuring cone in NGC 4921 is oriented such that the inner disc remains visible, and we argue that this geometric alignment may account for the variability in observed AGN properties. Furthermore, our results support the existence of a continuum between types 1 and 2 AGNs and indicate that water line observation is a effective method for detecting the inner accretion discs of type 2 AGNs.

This study introduces a framework that enables pre-training on a vast, unlabeled collection of real-world source code by leveraging data dependencies. Unlike standard autoencoding approaches that encode or decompose inputs token-by-token, our autoencoder operates at the function or method level. Specifically, we map each function or method to a vector representation based on its control-flow dependencies, derived from static program analysis. To reconstruct the original code, we employ two distinct neural language models: one utilizing word-level embeddings and the other function-level embeddings. Our secondary goal involves relearning the vector representations of function units to maximize reconstruction accuracy. Experimental results indicate that training on unlabeled source code equips pre-trained models with enhanced representations, allowing them to achieve strong results on various downstream tasks such as classification and defect detection without requiring additional labeling. Furthermore, comparison tests reveal that our proposed approach outperforms other pre-training strategies based on word-level embeddings, function-level embeddings, or a combination of both. Finally, applying this framework to a large Python dataset (over 92MB) demonstrates that the model can effectively reconstruct complex code segments. Our implementation and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/toidakahmard/code-pre-training.

Building on the Graphical Lasso method introduced by (Friedman 2007) for sparse inverse covariance estimation, this approach leverages coordinate descent to efficiently handle various graph constraints. The library is founded on (Ng and Liu 2014)'s algorithm, which employs Frobenius norm re-weighting to resolve constrained optimization tasks, a step crucial for maintaining sparsity in the solution. We compare GGLasso with other prominent software for both constrained and unconstrained Graphical Lasso problems, using 13 real-world datasets across 23 independent experiments. Our findings indicate that while many experiments yielded similar results across libraries, GGLasso consistently outperformed competitors in 4 out of 23 cases. Furthermore, we demonstrate through 22 separate tests that GGLasso achieves superior sparsity compared to competing libraries in 7 out of 22 experiments. A primary advantage of GGLasso lies in its support for a wide range of graph constraints, including those for sparse inverse covariance and precision matrices, which can be tailored to specific domain knowledge. Additionally, the library's implementation relies on the Ceres Solver (Agarwal 2016) for solving linear and quadratic systems, ensuring it can manage larger real-world datasets with minimal modifications. Finally, we illustrate that the library is adaptable to multiple objectives, such as maximizing matrix density and incorporating regularization terms like L1, cyclic group Lasso (cyclicgroup), mixed L1/L2 (elastic net), and graph cut (graphcut), as described by (Das 2013). While the original paper requested no comparisons, we conducted an evaluation against other libraries to demonstrate the sparsity of GGLasso's solutions on real-world datasets.

Finally, this approach will significantly constrain the unknown minimum mass of dark planets. While various algorithms exist for each of these individual tasks, we introduce a novel method that unifies all three into one cohesive procedure. This approach is effective for analyzing pre-recorded speech as well as in real-time scenarios. Speech recognition on mobile devices can be significantly improved by adapting to local accents and environments. Since multiple acoustic models are required to handle such variations, a Bayesian framework is essential to manage uncertainty regarding the specific model to utilize. We propose a novel Bayesian approach for adapting automatic speech recognition on mobile devices. This framework treats fundamental frequency, noise characteristics, and noise suppression capabilities as random variables, selecting parameters based on their most probable values. An online mechanism estimates these parameters in real-time, while a Bayesian mechanism calculates parameter means according to a specified prior distribution and information density. This enables rapid convergence within a few seconds. Experimental results indicate that our Bayesian framework achieves faster convergence within ten seconds compared to conventional methods. Consequently, the proposed Bayesian framework is highly suitable for mobile devices. Keywords: Mobile Phone, Accent, Accent Adaptation, Acoustic Model Selection, Noise, Mobile Environment, Bayesian Approach, Parameter Selection, Fundamental Frequency, Speech Recognition.

The primary objective of DWIFOB is to efficiently solve for the primal variables and the Lagrangian multiplier associated with the constraints in such problems. It examines the lepton flavor violating decays $l_i \to l_j \gamma$ in the context of two singlet extension of the NMSSM. These approaches share a key limitation: they are highly sensitive to noise within training data or algorithms, often resulting in structures that fail to converge. This vulnerability stems from their reliance on extensive numbers of iterations to maximize objective function values. In contrast, Bayesian optimization offers a more efficient framework for optimizing black-box functions. It constructs a surrogate model of the objective function and employs an acquisition function to choose the next evaluation point. This paper introduces a noise-robust Bayesian optimization algorithm, named Acquisition Function Acquisitions by Expected Improvement with Constraint (AFECI), which integrates constraints to streamline the search process and enhance efficiency. Our findings demonstrate that AFECI achieves a 4.01% improvement over the EF12 architecture and a 0.30% improvement over VGG16 when task loss is minimized. These results suggest that AFECI generates more efficient architectures under low loss conditions. Furthermore, AFECI exhibits superior performance compared to standard Bayesian optimization methods like EI and UCB when acquisition function noise is high. This confirms that incorporating constraints into the optimization process makes the algorithm more resilient to data noise. Ultimately, AFECI not only secures higher objective function values but also produces architectures with lower parametric counts. Finally, AFECI is applicable to various other optimization challenges.

This study addresses dynamic orchestration in NDN-based networks where nodes execute applications with varying degrees of input-specificity (IO-light or IO-heavy) and demand different latency thresholds for successful completion. Latency in this context refers to the ratio of packet interest transmission to data packets. We introduce a virtualization-aware scheduling algorithm designed for distributed, IO-heavy NDN networks. Furthermore, we develop analytical models to evaluate the performance of both IO-light and IO-heavy applications under different work-conserving scheduling policies. Analysis of these models reveals a trade-off between data propagation efficiency and computational task completion times. Our findings indicate that: 1) IO-light applications achieve higher completion rates but experience longer execution times, whereas IO-heavy applications exhibit the opposite trend; 2) Employing multiple computing devices within an NDN architecture enhances successful execution rates for both application types. These results provide a theoretical foundation for designing highly efficient distributed NDN systems. To validate our analytical models, we implemented a simulation using a custom-built C-based library. The simulation results align closely with our analytical findings. a stretched Euler–Bernoulli beam defined on a star-shaped metric graph with three identical edges. The edges are hinged at their outer vertices, while the central vertex allows for both translation and rotation. A singular spring connecting the central vertices is modeled as friction-like (proportional to the velocity vector). We provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the generator associated with the second-order PDE to be bounded below and ensure that all solutions decay exponentially over time. Since the system possesses an $SO(2)$ symmetry, we analyze a co-invariant subspace to reduce the problem to a set of coupled first-order ordinary differential equations. This analytical approach is supplemented by a complementary study of a discrete system formed by spatially discretizing each edge with a finite element. In this discrete context, we determine the conditions required for the system matrix to be positive (or semi-positive) definite, a criterion that is known to be sufficient for exponential stability in standard dissipative setups. Finally, we compare the findings from both the continuous and discrete analyses. Specifically, we observe that in the discrete case, the condition requiring the spring connection between the central vertices to be sufficiently strong becomes independent of the number of discretization nodes and strictly necessary for exponential stability, whereas a similar claim cannot be established for the continuous system. Furthermore, by formulating and solving an optimization problem, we demonstrate that a specific formulation of the spring potential allows the decay rate of the solutions to approach that of a rigid beam until a critical threshold is reached, at which point the decay rate becomes constant. This contrasts with a point mass connection (equivalent to an infinitely strong spring), which minimizes the decay rate by a factor of two. These insights are expected to prove valuable for designing robust extension mechanisms in applications involving beams that must remain straight. Keywords: Exponential stability, Euler-Bernoulli beam, star-shaped graph, singular spring, positive definite matrix, finite element method, beam extension mechanism.

In a concurrent study, the authors introduced, learned, and integrated a model of decision-maker (DM) utility into an item recommendation system, demonstrating that this method surpasses both existing multi-objective and standard rank-based (i.e., SVD) strategies. This paper details the implementation of the described system. DMs engage with the system via a mobile application, inputting ranked items of interest. The system responds with 20 recommended items out of a potential pool of 1,000. Our primary objective is to maximize DM utility as measured by their interaction with the recommended items. To achieve this, we employ a rank-based utility function. However, as noted in [1], a single, fixed DM utility function is often inadequate for interactions exceeding a few items. Consequently, we present a novel rank-based utility function designed to accommodate multiple DM preferences. We frame the problem of learning this function as a multi-player game between the system and the DM, referred to as the Preference game. Solving this game yields a recommended item set. To maximize system utility, we propose two strategies for participating in the Preference game: (a) Myopic Strategy, where the system acts greedily in each game round, and (b) System-wide Strategy, where the system plays optimally across all game rounds. Our results indicate that these proposed strategies significantly outperform both standard system approaches and the state-of-the-art method for multi-player games. Additionally, we propose a new approach for evaluating system performance against multi-player strategies, along with a method for comparing this to standard solutions in the rank-based domain. This paper serves as a full version, expanding upon the earlier short version [1] by incorporating four new experiments. While the short version maintained a fixed UCF dataset of 20 items per DM, the expanded version gradually increases the DM's item set to 40, 60, and 80 units. Furthermore, the full version integrates a new experiment focusing on the impact of system learning on utility function performance. This framework is relevant to high-$T_c$ superconductors, which possess a quarter-filled non-bonding band, as well as to various two-dimensional lattice models. Using a $k$-space mean-field approach, we analyze the spin nematic phase, a state defined by non-vanishing quadrupolar spin fluctuations alongside zero net spin and charge densities. Our findings indicate that a spin nematic phase exists near the band center, characterized by low-energy nematic quadrupolar fluctuations with a well-defined wave vector, $Q$. Furthermore, at the band center, the spin-nematic to ferromagnetic transition occurs at a higher critical temperature than the spin-nematic to paramagnetic transition. These results highlight the significance of nematic quadrupolar fluctuations in the emergence of low-energy ferromagnetic fluctuations, a phenomenon widely accepted as a precursor to high-$T_c$ superconductivity. Additionally, we investigate the impact of a periodic charge modulation with a $Q$-wave vector on these transitions. We demonstrate that in a spin-nematic system, a charge density wave phase with a finite order parameter can arise if the energy cost to double the electron concentration at nematic fluctuations with a $Q$-wave vector is negative. This scenario aligns with experimental observations in high-$T_c$ cuprates, where short-range charge modulations with a wave vector of approximately $(\pm\frac{1}{2}\pm\frac{1}{2})\pi$ have been detected at low temperatures within a non-magnetic state near the antiferromagnetic phase boundary. Our analysis reveals that the system's ground state corresponds to a spin-nematic state accompanied by a charge modulation of the same wave vector, consistent with the "Nematic-Cuprate" phase diagram recently proposed for high-$T_c$ superconductors. Finally, the feasibility of a spin-nematic phase is validated comparison with the results from a real-space analysis. Key elements of this work will be detailed in an upcoming, more extensive publication. Throughout this report, we utilize a non-interacting model with a half-filled anti-bonding band to illustrate the fundamental physics of these phenomena. In this setting, both reward functions and state transition kernels are unknown and permitted to change arbitrarily over time, subject to a constraint on their cumulative variations. The study introduces a novel algorithm termed TS-KLTSB, which is proven to achieve a regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{Tb(\log T)^2})$, where $T$ represents the total episode count and $b$ denotes the bound on variation for both the reward function and state transitions. Furthermore, a lower bound of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{Tb(\log T)})$ is established for any potentially suboptimal algorithm under similar conditions, demonstrating that the upper bound derived is nearly tight. The analysis reveals that the dependence on the parameter $b$ in both theoretical guarantees arises from the need to adapt to shifts in the risk attitude of the decision maker. Notably, if the changes in risk attitude are bounded a priori, the upper and lower bounds converge to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ and $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}}$ respectively, a result consistent with existing literature. These findings indicate that the proposed algorithm is optimal in addressing non-stationary problems where risk attitudes may also undergo temporal variations.

We start by introducing a general framework for DML over communication graphs, accommodating various stochastic averaging strategies. Because these infinite-dimensional problems frequently lack known analytical solutions, numerical methods are required to find approximate answers. This paper introduces a unified notation to describe key techniques within the transcription phase of simultaneous direct methods (specifically the discretize-then-optimize approach) for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization problems. The discussion highlights collocation, integrated residual, and Runge-Kutta schemes. A core advantage of this set of notations is its applicability to both mathematical formulation and the development of software for practical industrial problems. The paper also addresses the regularization of collocation constraints, explores techniques for handling stiff dynamics, and examines Appell’s 1890 method for reducing the number of collocation points in discretize-then-optimize problems featuring redundant dynamics. Finally, the study reviews Appell's original mathematical contributions to dynamical systems and provides a brief history of the evolution of collocation methods.

The study examines a broad category of non-coercive NLS systems in three dimensions that admit standing wave solutions of the form $\psi(x,t) = e^{i\omega t}\varphi(x)$. This reduces the problem to finding ground states $\psi^*_ { \omega }$ as minimizers of the energy functional $Q[u]=\int |\nabla x|^2dx- \lambda \int |x|p dx$ over the Sobolev space $H^1_0$, subject to the constraint $\|\psi\|^2= \int |\psi|^2dx=1$. This paper demonstrates that for a wide range of $\lambda >0$ and all $1< p<5/3$, a significantly broader class of non-coercive NLS systems admit ground states. This section introduces different MD approaches and describes the atomic theory employed in CP2K. 2.1 Ab-initio MD vs. Molecular Mechanics MD. Atomic motion in MD is governed by a series of tiny time steps. A fundamental distinction in CP2K is the treatment of electrons. ab-initio MD (ab-initio quantum nuclear dynamics) involves sampling the potential energy surface (PES) of an electronic system at 0 K, known as the ground state. Conversely, molecular mechanics MD or classical MD treats atoms as a collection of point charges and nuclei. A key attribute of molecular mechanics is the use of an effective nuclear charge to represent the electronic contribution to nuclear-nuclear interactions. This effective charge is derived from the ground-state electronic configuration of the system, calculated as a zeroth-order perturbation of the full electronic problem. This foundational work on molecular mechanics was done by R. Ahlswedter [2], forming the basis for the Car-Parrinello method (CP-MD) and the Born-Oppenheimer MD (BOMD) found in CP2K. The Car-Parrinello method is a semi-empirical approach where nuclei move under the influence of valence electrons, treated as a separate system with its own effective potential energy surface. Furthermore, we in-depth analyze the impact of different parameters, including eraser size, number of erasers, removal of context, and learning objectives. In this work, we propose a path toward quantifying complexity in seemingly generic quadratic Hamiltonians by analyzing the transition to q-deformed non-Gaussian statistics. We demonstrate that in the low-lying regime, the scaling of complexity is intrinsically linked to both the system's finite size and its entanglement entropy. Furthermore, near the ground state, complexity is equivalent to the Regge slope of the entanglement entropy as a function of the number of regions partitioning the spatial manifold. From the holographic standpoint, this relationship implies that the higher-spin charge of the black hole, characterized by a slightly non-Gaussian dual field theory, can be directly read off from the Regge slope of the entanglement wedge volume. Additionally, we examine the thermodynamic limit of the quadratic Hamiltonian, revealing a connection to universal features of the free fermion Sykese model. In this context, we also investigate the role of higher-spin charges derived from non-Gaussian statistics and their relationship to the Regge slope of the entanglement wedge within the dual holographic framework. Finally, we explore the implications of this relationship for the Regge trajectory of the bulk gravity theory. Any parallels between the low-lying limit and the thermodynamic limit suggest a universal structure in how we define or comprehend quantum complexity. These findings may offer a pathway to bridge the gap between the high-temperature description of the Schwinger–Keldysh contour in holographic models and the low-temperature ground state. More broadly, they hint at a method to quantify or constrain the complexity of the semi-classical quantum state corresponding to a black hole. that influence particle physics and cosmology. This note explores the scenario where two particle physics sectors exist within the visible brane, a phenomenon known as doublet-triplet hybridism. We name this specific scenario on two accounts: first, because a hidden sector exists in addition to the standard Model sector, and second, because the solution to the hierarchy problem remains intact. Constraining such a setup is difficult due to a lack of data, but we demonstrate that it is feasible by employing a simple supergravity model. Specifically, we address how to fine-tune the cosmological constant within the Minkowski regime, ensuring that all low-energy constants derived from the Kähler potential and superpotential are consistent with current experimental limits. Since our supergravity model incorporates both hedgehog monopoles and instantons, we calculate their one-loop contribution to the cosmological constant. Our analysis reveals that the contribution from hedgehogs is negligible in the one-loop approximation, whereas instantons provide a non-negligible contribution, allowing for the achievement of Minkowski space, thus resolving the hierarchy problem. Furthermore, we show that the proposed doublet-triplet hidden sector scenario can successfully achieve successful cosmological inflation, maintain stability, and break all necessary symmetries, including R-symmetry, while generating the necessary baryon number violation for successful baryogenesis. Therefore, we conclude that the doublet-triplet hidden sector scenario is viable, and we assign a star rating of ★★ to it. Finally, we address gravity-mediated supersymmetry mediation, demonstrating how real tree-level SUSY can be achieved with the lightest supersymmetric particle serving as a dark matter candidate, all within a stringy framework. In summary, we establish that the hierarchy problem is addressed, gravity-mediated SUSY mediation functions correctly, and natural dark matter is established, confirming that solving the cosmological inconsequence problem is equivalent to solving the hierarchy problem. We also establish that triple splitting in the dark sector is possible, confirming that mirror symmetry is not required to accomplish these goals. We further establish that preheating is effective and confirm that all anomalies are cancelled, proving that the Spontaneous Ecletism Hypothesis is correct. In closing, we establish the Two Higgs Doublet Model with two singlets, proving the correctness of complex dark energy, the correctness of the flexagon, and the validity of the cosmological preheating mechanism. and collaborate on open-source projects. To promote these initiatives, contributors need timely feedback on their code, which is often achieved through peer code reviews. However, not all projects maintain this standard; a survey of a random sample of repositories from the second half of 2019 revealed that only 15% explicitly require code reviews, while 36% leave the decision to maintainers or contributors without specific guidelines. This study examines the impact of mandatory reviews and the factors influencing the creation and content of pull requests (PRs) in a large-scale controlled experiment involving nearly 60 repositories across three domains within the Google Chrome project. By analyzing nearly 15,000 PRs over three years experimentally across various repositories of differing sizes and contributions, we found that making code reviews mandatory improves review quality but significantly increases the time PRs remain open. Specifically, the average review latency rises by 2.2 days (p < 0.001), and the time PRs remain pending before merging increases by 5.1 days (p < 0.001). Additionally, we observed no significant impact on the probability of PR acceptance or rejection. Furthermore, we discovered that the difficulty of a PR significantly influences its content and how easily it is reviewed, with harder PRs exhibiting higher review latency. Finally, we investigated the role of contributor expertise: less experienced contributors produced higher-quality reviews, yet both contributors and reviewers experienced longer delays due to the review process. These findings offer valuable insights for developers designing new projects or updating those with a culture discouraging mandatory reviews, as the experiment demonstrates that making reviews compulsory significantly impacts the PR lifecycle. Given the experiment's scale and duration, our results are statistically significant and generalize across multiple systems, suggesting that these conclusions may apply to other large-scale systems with similar characteristics. This research was supported by an industry-student partnership between Brown and the Google Chrome open-source project, ensuring our findings can be directly applied to real-world systems. This work was performed under the author's PhD thesis at the Google Chrome open-source project. The experiment concluded in December 2021. Nevertheless, conventional single-target or dual-target CDR approaches are limited by two key issues: the unrealistic assumption that a user's activity patterns remain uniform across different domains, and an overlooked bias toward high-rated items in existing multi-target CDR models. To address these limitations, we introduce the Target and Rating Activity-PatternAware Recommender (T-Rec). A rating bias adjustment module further refines the continuous user embeddings to boost recommendation accuracy. We evaluated T-Rec across three real-world datasets spanning three target domains. Comparison with state-of-the-art models demonstrates that T-Rec significantly outperforms them, with statistical tests confirming its superiority. Additionally, case studies illustrate how T-Rec effectively resolves the activity and rating challenges specific to each domain. Case analyses highlight the model's capacity to handle domain-specific variations, and an interview assessed T-Rec's interpretability, showing strong agreement with our design assumptions. Overall, T-Rec not only delivers high accuracy but also provides transparency and explainability through its intelligent pattern learning. Case studies and interviews demonstrate that these features make T-Rec more user-friendly and capable of improving satisfaction. We analyze conductance fluctuations in the unitary regime, where the conduction electron density $n$ approaches the effective magnetic field $b$ ($n \sim b$), within a two-dimensional electron gas (2D214) at high magnetic fields. Variance and skewness measurements align well with weak conduction electron effects. At the metal-insulator transition, an intensity burst in the conductance spectrum occurs at low frequencies. The background level of these bursts varies with the $n/b$ ratio and disappears near the transition. A quantitative explanation for these findings is achieved by combining the random self-consistent field (RSCF) method with the size-dependent line shape approach by Shmueli and Mello. This framework predicts burst conductivity at frequencies $w \sim v_k/k_F l$ and provides explanations for the dependence on $n$, $b$, and the sample size $L$. Additionally, the model successfully explains the suppression of background conductance as $L$ increases. The resulting skewness indicates that bursts arise from conduction electrons trapped by impurities. Since the frequency at which bursts disappear corresponds to the group velocity equaling the mean free path $L \sim v_k l$, these conductance bursts can serve as a tool for investigating the silicon carbide transition. Furthermore, the RSCF+Mello approach offers a means to explore the role of local moments in fractional quantum effects.

An OGS is defined by the property that every group element can be uniquely expressed as a product of specific power sequences associated with its generators, where the exponents exist within a particular restricted domain. This article explores OGSs for p-groups by addressing two primary objectives. First, we establish bounds regarding the maximum length of an OGS; while Ostrowski's classical result confirms a OGS always exists for abelian p-groups, our work demonstrates that for non-abelian p-groups, the OGS length does not surpass $3(P+1)^2$, where $P$ denotes the highest prime power exponent in the group's element orders. This finding is tied to a positive resolution of a query posed by P.M. Cohn in 1964. Second, we investigate necessary and sufficient conditions for a group to possess a generator of the form $(g_1, \dots, g_m), (g_1^{\alpha_1}, \dots, g_m^{\alpha_m})$. Our results indicate that for non-abelian p-groups, the OGS length is bounded by $4(p+1)^3$. Furthermore, we provide explicit examples of p-groups where this bound must be exact. These groups feature a commutator subgroup with a specific structure and include a normal subgroup of prime power order composed of central generators, a configuration where the bound reaches $2(p+1)^3$. Additionally, we present a result indicating that if a p-group's commutator subgroup is trivial, the bound of $4(p+1)^3$ may still need to be upheld. Finally, we compile examples of p-groups where the bound can be tightened to $3(p+1)^2$. Groups exhibiting this refined bound are characterized by a particular structure within their commutator subgroups, specifically involving a cyclic subgroup of order $p$. We also examine an open question by Cohn from 1964, proving it is affirmative for OGSs with the bound $3(p+1)^2$ and discussing related open problems. scalar field theories involving two fields that lack $SO(2)$ invariance. A notable example of this class is the well-established Montonen-Sarker-Trullinger-Bishop model. These systems are significant because the $U(1)$ current fails to be conserved due to explicit symmetry-breaking terms in the action. We demonstrate the existence of kink solitons by analyzing a system of first-order ordinary differential equations. Despite the non-conservation of the $U(1)$ current, our methodology is sufficiently broad to examine soliton configurations in any generic two-field interacting scalar theory, and we further outline additional advantages of this approach. Finally, we calculate the monodromy matrix for the Montonen-Sarker-Trullinger-Bishop kink and explore a scenario involving two kinks with opposite charges. This setup is particularly relevant as it paves the way for studying soliton scattering. In subsequent research, we will utilize these findings to derive scattering coefficients for the monodromy matrix of this theory. Our findings will eventually enable the reconstruction of the full $S$-matrix for interacting two-field scalar theories. Additionally, we have examined the monodromy matrix for a generic two-field theory using the algebraic data method, as detailed in our other published work. In that study, we showed how to determine the full interaction matrix from the monodromy matrix of two kinks; since the monodromy for this specific model can be readily computed, the $S$-matrix for the Montonen-Sarker-Trullinger-Bishop theory can now be determined. This research extends our earlier studies on constructing the $S$-matrix for generic two-field scalar field theories, which previously relied on solving nonlinear differential equations. Our approach is advantageous as it applies to a broader range of theories, including those with non-linear scalar coupling. Looking ahead, this general framework can be extended to accommodate gauge-invariant theories. In such cases, the method remains fully functional for constructing the $S$-matrix if the $U(1)$ charge is not dynamically coupled. This includes relevant applications in baryon number non-conservation and the study of cosmic strings. Furthermore, our findings regarding two-kink monodromy may prove useful in future work on the dynamical monodromy matrix for $SU(2)$ bimeron-bimeron scattering. Ultimately, this research utilizes the monodromy matrix of two kinks to fully determine the $S$-matrix for two-dimensional interacting scalar field theories

However, the situation regarding different types of SDEs and their associated probabilistic formulations is more complex. This paper introduces the concept of $\kappa$-regularity and examines its implications. Specifically, we demonstrate that the commonly used Milstein approximation for Feller-Diffusion type SDEs achieves an overall convergence rate of $\overline{O(\delta^\frac{2}{\kappa})}$ in the supremum norm, where $\kappa \in \{1,2,3\}$. Notably, this result implies a convergence rate of $O(\delta^{2-\epsilon})$ in the supremum norm for solutions of the linear stochastic heat equation, a Diffusion type SDE, and the associated stochastic heat equation. These findings represent the first convergence rates for these specific SDEs that exceed the standard $O(\delta)$ rate. Furthermore, our approach yields explicit error bounds without relying on norm inequalities like Cauchy-Schwartz. While achieving superconvergence rates of $O(\delta^{2-\epsilon})$ for SDEs is a new achievement, obtaining such rates for the associated PDEs is entirely novel. Our methodology is explicit and applies to a broad class of SDEs exhibiting a balance between their drift and diffusion. In contrast, implicit numerical schemes such as the Roelofsen-Timmerman method appear less promising for achieving superconvergence in either type. Finally, the expected error in the $L^2$ norm is $O(\delta^\frac{1}{\kappa})$.

While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (reminos). This software enables the automated \textit{ad hoc} inclusion of every possible combination of a new PDF prediction across all relevant data sets. This represents a significant methodological advancement, as it eliminates nearly all manual efforts related to combining multiple calculations and experimental data, thereby facilitating the rapid and straightforward determination of global $\chi^2$ values for all candidate PDFs. Finally, we present a complete NLO NLLLL global fit using a limited set of data and a varying number of \textit{combination} papers for PDFs from different groups, highlighting how \textit{combination} streamlines the calculation and greatly enhances its accessibility. The Holographic Entropy Cone (HEC) comprises the range of permissible entropies defined by Riesz's type of strong subadditivity. This study investigates the entropy regions formed by the intersection of the HEC with the set of multivariate nonnegativity constraints derived from the Carlen-Georgiou Maurey (CMM) inequalities and their extensions. We demonstrate that the resulting region exhibits a conical structure and presents a conjecture asserting its finite generation. Furthermore, we propose an entropic inequality that, when integrated with the CMM inequalities, yields a tighter upper bound on multipartite entropy. This tighter bound is strictly negative for specific low-partite partitions and remains negative for various low-partite partitions involving high particity. We also examine the influence of negative entropy contributions on the magnitude of negative multipartite entropy. Entropic regions characterized by all negative multipartite entropies are identified as the most efficient testers for the finite generation conjecture. Finally, we outline the future research agenda required to elucidate the fundamental geometry of the finite generation conjecture.

In the most efficient model, the client sends only a few classical bits per round, while the server performs all quantum operations. We examined this problem when the server's quantum capabilities are unbounded, meaning the client cannot rely on the server's quantum limitations for security. In standard "soliton" configurations, larger outer disks shield smaller inner ones from direct collisions with the channel walls. We introduce a novel class of unsymmetric "anti-soliton" configurations, where the outer disks are the smallest, allowing the central disk to collide with the walls. While this anti-soliton motion eventually ceases, we derive a closed-form expression for the total collision count. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for certain parameter set-ups, this count diverges to infinity, with the largest disks acting as a protective barrier against wall collisions for the smallest disks. This anti-soliton dynamics, where the central disk directly strikes the walls and energy dissipation is proportional to impact velocity, serves as a minimal example of a system that transitions from integrable to non-integrable behavior when moved from a stationary to a accelerated frame of reference. Numerical simulations utilize a piecewise linear approximation of inelastic dissipation grounded in the coefficient of restitution. Given that this anti-soliton motion experiences a threefold increase in the acceleration coefficient due to its non-integrable nature in accelerated frames, these findings are highly relevant to the "shake-sort" experiment, which aims to order disks by size using a shaking table (equivalent to a vertically accelerated frame) that transitions from vertical to horizontal. Current soliton-based shake-sort experiments achieve ordering efficiency in the tens; our anti-soliton initial conditions offer the prospect of significantly higher efficiency, potentially improving current results by a factor of at least five. Additionally, anti-solitons provide both an analytically exact method to determine the critical acceleration threshold and a way to investigate the dependence of ordering efficiency on this threshold. The set of "forbidden frequencies" that prevent ordering within a time T scales with T in the vertical frame but shifts to a region near the critical frequency in the horizontal frame. Finally, we propose a strategy to extend the oscillation duration of the anti-soliton system. Extending the acceleration phase vertically can increase the oscillation period hundredfold, effectively "compressing" the oscillation within a millimeter. Trapping an anti-soliton in a vertical channel above the acceleration threshold allows it to oscillate for an effectively infinite amount of time. distinct flavors of El Niño—the East Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP)/Modoki types—affect global climate variability. While many prior studies relied on linear multivariate statistics or composite analysis, this paper introduces a Bayesian statistical approach, applying it for the first time to a binary classification problem to distinguish between EP and CP El Niño events. This novel Bayesian method offers several distinct benefits: unlike dependent composite analyses that are often restricted to a fixed number of categories, the Bayesian classifier can differentiate among any count of classes; it circumvents the need for extensive pre-processing, rendering it immune to issues like outliers, non-linearity, or elliptical distributional assumptions; and it yields optimal results when classes exhibit the maximum separation. This study demonstrates that, similar to earlier findings, EP El Niños produce more pronounced sea surface temperature anomalies in the western Pacific and stronger impacts on eastern Pacific sea level temperatures. Furthermore, the new procedure is capable of anticipating the specific flavor of an El Niño event prior to its full maturity, a capability that previous statistical techniques largely lacked. This Bayesian-based classification technique represents a fresh and potentially superior method compared to existing classifications, showing potential for future monitoring and prediction efforts. Finally, the paper calculates the Bayes risk for both classification systems to quantify the misclassification error rate, assessing the performance of both the traditional and proposed Bayesian classifiers. Keywords: Bayesian classifier, Bayes risk, El Niño.

We present a potentially significant observational indicator of MBH formation within dwarf galaxies: a continuous mass spectrum of MBHs in these systems. Our findings imply a possible universal "seed" mass for growing MBHs and offer a novel insight into the history of gas accretion in the early Universe. We anticipate that a similar analysis of the mass spectrum of MBHs in Local Group dwarfs, recently published, will soon confirm this "bottom-up" formation scenario in gas-rich, low-mass dwarfs. Ultimately, these results offer a fresh perspective on the nature of MBHs and their impact on galaxy evolution. I assess the viability of the wide binary test using the "line velocity" approach, which isolates velocity components along the sky plane aligned with the line connecting the two stars. This method was previously rejected for Newtonian gravity when applied to Accelerated Wave Gravity (AWG), a theory proposing a modification to Newtonian gravity driven by acceleration waves. By examining the sky plane relative velocity "line velocity" distributions from two specific WB samples, I compare the rejection significance under both theory and hypothesis using chi-squared ($\chi^2$) tests. Under AWG, the most significant test yields a 2$\sigma$ rejection, yet it requires a massive contribution of velocity data with uncertain reliability. Under the standard Newtonian gravity (NG) hypothesis, the NG vs. AWG test using the second WB sample achieves a 3.8$\sigma$ detection of NG, with a cross-test using the first sample reaching 4.2$\sigma$. Furthermore, age estimation via Gaia data indicates that all WB stars in these samples belong to different evolutionary stages, implying the combined samples likely represent more than half of the total population in any given area. These cross-theory results demonstrate a substantial increase in test power, providing an order of magnitude gain in 1-$\sigma$ sensitivity to relative velocities when distinguishing between NG and AWG. This allows $\Delta v_{line}$ tests to either confirm a previously feared "gap" near $0.2 c$ in the AWG spectrum or achieve a 5-$\sigma$ detection of AWG if the gap is due to the mixture of WB samples containing different old-age populations. We demonstrate that the circular motion of ions generates a dynamic magnetoelectric effect, providing a coupling between electric and magnetic dipole moments. This phenomenon occurs specifically when a non-centrosymmetric crystal exhibits a spin distorting mode. Using first-principles calculations, we identify this terahertz magnetoelectric effect in the helimagnet CrTe. CrTe features intermetallic-like circular electron orbits in the terahertz frequency range, which significantly strengthen the magnetoelectric coupling. We predict that Cr's helical spin and electric dipole moments can be effectively controlled via either terahertz magnetic or electric field pulses. Furthermore, we show that this generalized magnetoelectric effect represents a circularly polarized terahertz emission with far-field components for both magnetic and electric dipole moments, and it converts incident circularly polarized terahertz radiation into voltage signals. This represents the first observation of a terahertz magnetoelectric effect driven by spin excitations on a crystal lattice. We anticipate that similar effects will occur in various other non-centrosymmetric materials when their spin excitations align with their vibrational modes. Our findings suggest that terahertz magnetoelectric emitters and sensors/sensors can be realized in Cr's helimagnetic chromium-telluride. Our proposed terahertz magnetoelectric material, CrTe, serves as a sensitive detector for circularly polarized terahertz waves with a wavelength of approximately 30 micrometers. Research in this domain often assumes access to a complete set of activity instances, typically collected via paper-based or digital checklists. However, in real-world scenarios, many instances remain unreported, and the challenges of retrieving them are compounded by the intermittent and irregular nature of data submission. Furthermore, existing approaches are highly inflexible; they depend on a fixed sequence of reporting steps defined at the process's start, whereas actual executions are often more ad-hoc. This paper introduces Bayesian Update Games, a novel model for reasoning about semi-structured processes from incomplete activity instances. Unlike traditional methods, this model allows for a dynamic sequence of reporting steps, even when specific instances are missing. We demonstrate that while Bayesian Update Games are computationally complex—precluding closed-form solutions for optimal strategies—we can efficiently approximate them using reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we show that optimal strategies can be derived by making reasonable assumptions about unreported instances. Finally, we validate our model using a real-world dataset of approximately 400 instances from an emergency response process. Our findings indicate that even with a significant portion of activity instances unreported, accurate state estimates can be achieved with a limited number of reports. This work has already been accepted for publication in ICPR 2021.

Smoking a cigar exposes a person to approximately 2,500 mg of particulate matter (PM), which exists as a mixture of elemental carbon (EC), organic carbon (OC), primary particulate matter (primary PM), and secondary particulate matter (secondary PM). Distinguishing between these components is crucial for evaluating the health risks of cigar smoking. This study employs an advanced uptake model, specifically the "boxes in a line" model, to calculate EC/EC+OC for secondhand tobacco smoke (SHS) and EC/EC+OC in primary PM. By combining this model with EC measurements from both primary PM and total PM in wildfire smoke, we isolate the concentrations of OC in primary PM and OC in secondary PM. Results indicate that the OC concentration in primary PM from secondhand cigar smoke ranges from 1,100 to 2,300 times that of EC, while OC in secondary PM is between 10 and 20 times the EC concentration. Furthermore, we developed a calculation for particulate matter toxicity based on the theory that higher EC content correlates with greater toxicity, demonstrating that both primary PM and secondary PM from secondhand cigar smoke are highly toxic, a finding that contradicts assumptions made in prior research. Consequently, this study provides new insights into the harmful effects of secondhand cigar smoke, which could inform future public health policies. We introduce a privacy framework based on Rényi divergence to bound the expected loss of privacy for conditionally dependent data. This approach leverages a bound on the Rényi entropy of the remaining unknown data, accounting for the viewer's prior knowledge. The framework is particularly useful in scenarios where a viewer possesses a specific model of data dependencies among users. We demonstrate this with two instances: first, a dependent model applicable to a user's home location, and second, a spatially correlated model where users' locations depend on each other's positions relative to them. We show that, under spatial correlation, maintaining privacy is more challenging as the number of users increases, whereas with the dependent model, increasing the number of users can actually enhance privacy. Furthermore, we develop a Markov-based model to estimate the impact of data dependence on privacy loss for specific users within a group exhibiting spatial correlation, enabling the creation of an approximate dependent model for users with high potential privacy loss. We validate this approximation's efficacy by implementing it in a system designed to automatically suggest dependent datasets for public consumption. This system selects appropriate datasets for users to disclose to achieve significant privacy goals, even when multiple users are present. The choice of a dependent dataset triggers the adoption of a dependent model, which adjusts the type of data assumed to be dependent on a user's profile. Additionally, we find that discelling a dependent dataset prevents a significant increase in the probability of spatial correlation, thereby spatially distributing users and reducing travel costs. This allows for the inference of dependent datasets without necessarily compromising the privacy of individual users. The dependent datasets available in our implementation can be accessed here.

Fisher introduced the concept of reproductive value. This paper offers a continuous-time framework for this value. We provide a novel proof of Fisher's Fundamental Theorem, demonstrating that selection pressure equals the weighted covariance between a trait and reproductive rate, where weights correspond to reproductive value. This formulation elucidates the influence of spatial heterogeneity on genetic drift. We further present an alternative derivation of the theorem using large-scale limit theories for stochastic processes. In this context, reproductive value emerges from the duality between Poisson processes and their intensities. Additionally, we extend the theorem to polygenic traits by defining polygenic reproductive value. Our analysis reveals that the polygenic component of drift comprises a large deterministic term and a stochastic term of natural logarithmic scale. These findings underscore the critical role of reproductive value in understanding allele frequency dynamics. Key words: Fisher's Fundamental Theorem, reproductive value, infinitesimal model, population genetics, IGLT, Haldane's diffusion, duality, Poisson process, stochastic partial differential equation.

Short Answer: While Fisher established the link between variance in selection and the tempo of evolutionary change, the expected trajectory of a trait under the infinitesimal model was later defined by the linkage dynamics proposed by Mendel and Le Cam. This work introduces a method to track linkage via stochastic spatial reproduction kernels. However, reproductive influence is better understood by analyzing variances in evolutionary pressure. This study offers a fresh perspective on Fisher's work and extends it to continuous-time "large" models. Although Fisher linked variance in selection to reproductive value, this research demonstrates that reproductive value can be more insightfully expressed through the analysis of first moments. This approach yields new perspectives on evolutionary trajectories and highlights the impact of stochasticity in evolutionary change. These results depend on solving a continuous-time "option pricing" problem known as the Black-Scholes equation, a challenge addressed using duality techniques that also reveal insights into reproductive value. This enables a precise description of first moments in continuous-time "large" populations. These findings support the view that longer ED stays are beneficial and suggest that patients requiring further observation or treatment should be transported home later. Furthermore, this approach helps address skepticism toward quantitative analyses and provides empirical support for a widely cited healthcare management principle. However, we observe that a significant increase in the length of stay does not consistently lead to improved survival rates. We conclude that extending the stay yields marginal survival improvements and that patients may derive multiple non-monetary intangible benefits from their ED experience. Most importantly, enhancing ED performance requires balancing the correlation between length of stay and survival, rather than prioritizing stay duration above all else. Finally, we recommend adopting newer statistical techniques for future research.

This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks supported by three levels of individual effort, where total work follows a Poisson distribution. We derive the optimal coordination strategy for a central planner, known as the centralized solution, and analyze a decentralized approach where agents independently pursue private payoffs based on team output. A key finding is that the Nash equilibrium of the decentralized game may significantly deviate from the centralized optimum, potentially leading to task undercompletion or redundancy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a single agent's behavioral change—adopting slightly more or less active tactics—can induce a discrete shift in the Nash equilibrium from inactivity to full engagement in a task. This occurs because strategic agents account for their interactive impacts on total work and the resulting payoffs. Consequently, even minor payoff adjustments can trigger discrete jumps in agent behavior. Our cross-fertilization of control and game-theoretic approaches offers a novel way to investigate coordination challenges. The insights derived here have broad implications for designing efficient teams in critical areas such as search and rescue, manufacturing, and data collection. Ultimately, this research highlights that efficient task completion does not necessitate a centralized planner.

crowdfunding, has drawn considerable scholarly attention. Unlike traditional sales models where businesses directly offer products or services in exchange for cash, crowdfunding involves raising small monetary contributions from a large number of individuals. This research examines the role of emotional content in crowdfunding campaigns using a dataset of 114,533 public funding requests. Our analysis reveals that while cognitive language enhances funding probability, emotional language exerting an inhibiting effect strengthens the value of cognitive speech. Furthermore, we evaluated the impact of auditory features; although speech rate and pitch demonstrated significant effects, non-verbal audio features like tone of voice were found to be highly critical. Specifically, the tone of voice exhibits an interacting effect with cognitive speech, indicating that auditory characteristics are as essential as textual content. Consequently, we propose that both text and non-verbal speech characteristics, particularly the tone of voice, are highly relevant in the context of crowdfunding. These findings carry substantial practical implications for funding platforms and entrepreneurs seeking to enhance their fundraising efforts. Consequently, funding platforms should encourage the inclusion of both verbal and non-verbal emotional content, while entrepreneurs should integrate these elements into their public funding requests. Furthermore, our results validate the feasibility of successfully collecting and analyzing large-scale, real-world crowdfunding datasets, a methodology that is applicable across various domains. Finally, our approach is fully open-source, enabling researchers to replicate the study on diverse types of crowdfunding campaigns. detecting network attacks within single organizations, developing an ML-based detection system using heterogeneous data from multiple sources remains a significant challenge. This difficulty stems primarily from privacy concerns, as sharing raw organization data violates user privacy. To address this, a decentralized framework is proposed. In this system, individual organizations train their own local decision models without exchanging sensitive data. Through a coordinated process involving data-independent communication, these local models are aggregated to form a comprehensive decision model. This research focuses on two key areas: first, applying a Bayesian Milieu to detect cyber-physical system (CPS) attacks in a decentralized manner, and second, extending this application to an energy network. The Bayesian Milieu approach demonstrates superior performance compared to a standard Bayesian model. Furthermore, the study evaluates the effectiveness of the decentralized system in identifying cyber-physical energy network attacks. Results indicate that the Bayesian Milieu outperforms the standard Bayesian approach, and the decentralized framework achieves higher accuracy than a centralized system that processes raw organization data. The study also confirms the method's robustness against communication failures. The application of a Bayesian Milieu in this context offers a novel contribution, and the findings from this rigorous evaluation hold significant importance for both research and practical implementations. While the paper emphasizes the detection of energy network cyber-physical attacks, the underlying Bayesian Milieu techniques are applicable to cyber-physical attacks across other domains as well. Keywords: Bayesian Milieu, Cyber-Physical Energy Network Attacks, Decentralized Machine Learning. However, current research assumptions lack realism, particularly the omission of acceleration and deceleration dynamics, which are critical when velocity constraints are active. By incorporating these dynamics, we develop a new approach to transform a heuristic-based sequence into a feasible one. We evaluate this method against the best existing feasible sequence generator on a multi-point manufacturing benchmark, demonstrating that our approach is efficient, scalable, and capable of reducing motion time by up to 3.43 times. Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark with realistic constraints, along with the necessary tools for calculating motion time and optimizing the controller parameters of a specific differential drive robot. This benchmark will facilitate the comparison of various optimization methods in future studies. a network of diverse oscillators, where members within each group align to a shared time evolution, while distinct groups evolve differently. This phenomenon has previously been studied under the assumption that systems within a group are identical and that inter-system couplings meet strict criteria. By relaxing these requirements to allow for approximate satisfaction, we demonstrate that stable group synchronization persists even when individual system parameters and coupling values deviate slightly from their nominal settings. Through a master stability function approach, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for stability in this scenario, a method that also enables the quantification of synchronization error. Furthermore, we examine stability in the presence of intra-group connections, extending existing literature by identifying a broader class of connection matrices that allow the stability problem to be reduced to a low-dimensional form. Across all studies, we observe that stability conditions become more stringent as the magnitude of parameter and coupling perturbations increases. This offers a robust framework for analyzing designed synchronization patterns in networks of real-world, non-identical oscillators, such as a power grid. Finally, we review design strategies for achieving group synchronization among non-identical systems and illustrate these results with numerical examples.

A key outcome is the identification of a strong upper bound of $0.27$ on the coefficient of the leading twist field. , limited research has addressed interference correlation, a factor that can significantly increase local delay—the number of time slots needed for a node to successfully transmit a packet. This study investigates the effects of interference correlation on three key areas: distributed transmission protocols, the design of asynchronous local coordination schemes, and the development of delayed transmission strategies. To do so, we introduce a graph-based analytical framework that captures interference correlation through the delay adjacency graph. Our results show that while most existing interference-independent protocols perform well in low-delay scenarios, they can degrade into exponential complexity and poor performance when delay correlation is present. To mitigate this, we propose two asynchronous local coordination schemes that are simpler, interference-resistant, and capable of achieving either high density or high delay-free throughput. Additionally, we present two delayed transmission protocols that leverage delay adjacency graphs for scheduled transmissions, successfully balancing density and delay objectives where other protocols fail. We validated these findings using both analytical models and wireless packet-trace simulations. Ultimately, this work provides a robust method for accurately characterizing interference correlation in real networks, thereby enabling the design of wireless protocols that perform exceptionally well under realistic interference conditions. Finally, we argue that delayed transmission protocols are more effective at addressing delay causation than correlation, yielding superior network performance.

In asynchronous ad-hoc networks, the complexity of interference correlation significantly hinders the creation of efficient distributed transmission protocols. We demonstrate that while most current approaches succeed with independent interference, they perform poorly when interference correlation is present. To overcome this, we introduce a delayed backoff protocol that guarantees both high packet density and low delay. Furthermore, we present a protocol based on asynchronous local coordination that achieves either high density or high delay-free throughput, depending on specific network requirements. We derived an upper bound on delay for delayed backoff and found it difficult to improve, suggesting protocol designers should shift focus from minimizing delay to maximizing packet density. Our asymptotic inter-node distance-based correlation model was validated through packet-trace simulations, and cross-validation with a more traditional MCDF model confirmed that our delayed backoff protocol is substantially more robust than any existing local coordination scheme.

Achieving high packet density in wireless ad-hoc networks often conflicts with the likelihood of successful transmission. We introduce a global adaptation protocol that regulates a node's transmission probability based on network size and density, utilizing a closed-form expression for the probability of first-order interference. We compare this approach with three popular local adaptation protocols, finding that local methods can stabilize only when interference is independent, low intensity, and sparsely correlated. state-of-the-art performance in graph classification tasks, yet their dependability remains a critical issue. This paper introduces a method to assess prediction confidence for graph classification using GNNs. The approach involves training a "shadow model"—a simpler, easier-to-analyze network—that learns to mimic the decisions of the primary GNN through supervised training. Using these trained shadow models, the study examines three techniques to estimate prediction confidence: scoring, feature attribution, and per-sample approximation of the label function. The proposed framework is capable of estimating confidence for any existing GNN architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared to traditional methods, the shadow model approach offers more accurate confidence estimates. Furthermore, the study shows that this technique can identify "high-confidence" samples suitable for safe automated labeling, thereby reducing the number of complex samples requiring expert annotation in semi-supervised scenarios. The performance of the approach was validated on three standard datasets: Cora, Citeseer, and Facebook. Sources for the Cora, Citeseer, and Facebook datasets can be found at https://www.cs.utexas.edu/users/liangz/datasets/ and https://data.challenge.istanbul/ for the Instagram dataset. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/zhuxiaodan98/ShadowModels_for_GNN. To ensure reproducibility, the shadow model approach significantly outperforms three baseline methods, including a simple linear model, feature attribution, and sign approximation. Importantly, this framework is designed to be versatile and can yield high-accuracy confidence estimates for "black-box" models without the need to retrain the primary GNNs, thereby saving expertise time in semi-supervised learning contexts. To our knowledge, this is the first approach dedicated to approximating the sign of the label function for individual samples. To summarize, the proposed shadow model framework: (1) accommodates any GNN architecture, (2) enhances confidence estimation accuracy compared to existing methods, and (3) enables the evaluation of "high-confidence" samples for automatic labeling by experts in semi-supervised learning. To conclude our approach, we introduce "ShadowNet," a straightforward shadow model variant trained to replicate the forward pass output of a given GNN instead of its class predictions. ShadowNet achieves the highest accuracy in confidence estimation among all tested methods using any GNN architecture. Additionally, ShadowNet requires no new training when a new black-box GNN is introduced; it can be trained in approximately one minute for every 1,000 validation samples. We introduce PatchNet, a streamlined convolutional neural network designed to match objects across consecutive video frames by learning patch-level correlation features rather than relying on pixel-level data. PatchNet is highly compact, operating at only 56 MFLOPs, which is four times more efficient than MobileNetV2. We applied PatchNet to video object detection and visual object tracking tasks, achieving an 8.75 MFPLOPs model that is four times smaller than PatchNet Core and a 2.3 times smaller detection model compared to MobileNetV2. Our experiments on video object detection and visual tracking datasets demonstrate that PatchNet outperforms its larger parent models in actual application performance. Specifically, on the YouTube-Faces dataset, PatchNet reaches a 93.5% detection mean accuracy with an inference time of 0.84 FPS. On the MOTChallenges dataset, it attains a 91.4% detection mean accuracy and 44.24 FPS. Furthermore, on the DMDS dataset, it achieves an 83.1% detection mean accuracy at 20.89 FPS. These results highlight PatchNet's highly efficient performance. Additionally, we developed a real-time tracking application using PatchNet at 44.24 FPS, which we plan to release publicly. We also provide a detection application that supports multiple object categories and 1080p resolution at 93.5% mean accuracy. All PatchNet models are available on GitHub. We anticipate that PatchNet and its associated applications will be valuable for object detection, tracking, and other video processing applications.

First, a distinct architecture is proposed where receivers harvest energy from an Access Point (AP) without requiring a signal splitter; in this OFDMA model, specific spectrum portions are allocated for Information Decoding (ID) while others are dedicated to Energy Harvesting (EH). To evaluate performance gains, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize harvested energy in a multi-user single-cell OFDMA downlink while ensuring minimum data-rate requirements are met for all users, solved via optimization tools to find a locally optimal solution where each user's rate is set to its minimum requirement. Second, the system model is refined to address practical challenges in implementing SWIPT OFDMA for both ID and EH, such as minimizing interference to reduce harmful noise for information reception and optimizing energy to lower input power to the APs. Finally, a downlink OFDMA scheme utilizing Power Splitting (PS) is introduced where the AP draws energy from a photovoltaic source; an optimization tool is used to determine the optimal power splitting ratio that minimizes the AP's input energy while satisfying all users' data-rate constraints. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed SWIPT OFDMA with optimized rate and PS schemes significantly boosts harvested energy by an average of 40% and slashed input power to the network APs by 30% compared to traditional CWIPT OFDMA with PS methods. These findings suggest that the introduced framework holds great promise for enhancing future high-speed optical-wireless communication networks, such as LiFi and FRS, which are currently being developed to create a true optical wireless bi-directional spectrum.

These vehicles navigate a city-based network, adapting their movement strategy based on the connected type of the adjacent block where their current block's occupancy threshold has been triggered. Using a complex network of blocks from a real Chinese city, we examine the complexity of the mobile agent system and introduce a "synergy" mechanism for adaptive evolution in their movement strategies. We analyze the system's complexity through entropy and the complexity measure $D_{C}$, as well as its "intelligent" performance via the average path length of the network. Results indicate that agent synergy evolves the movement strategy system into a near-critical state, raising the network's complexity while significantly lowering the average path length. Consequently, this complex network structure substantially boosts the system's robustness against random or targeted node attacks and makes it easier to locate hidden targets within the city network. This approach demonstrates that a MAM of Braitenberg vehicles can be a potent tool for urban exploration, traffic analysis, and solving the traveling salesman problem. Furthermore, we argue that introducing "intelligent" movement strategies and a learning mechanism for the vehicle system not only enhances the network complexity and reduces the average path length but also serves as a powerful method for optimizing connections in a real-world complex network. This research underscores the potential for applying the evolution of "intelligent" strategies in movement to various optimization problems. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the broader development of complex adaptive intelligent transportation systems. A video is available to illustrate the complexity of the Braitenberg vehicle-based MAM system and its papers.

multivariate Gaussian processes (GP). These processes are defined as multivariate extensions of univariate GPs, where each component is a random function or surface, and any finite set of samples follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution. However, in multivariate contexts, a single response may exhibit distinct dependence structures across different covariates, and the associated patterns may shift over time or space. Multivariate GPs can model such multivariate and temporal/spatial dependencies through a multivariate covariance function, which can be constructed in various ways. Despite this capability, covariance functions are usually estimated separately for each response, an approach that may hinder optimal accuracy given the ignored structure. Additionally, exact Gaussian likelihoods are computationally infeasible for large datasets, so approximate methods are required. We introduce a framework that (i) investigates multivariate dependency structures and (s)mooths varying covariance functions, implemented in the (ii)multivariate (GPVF) package. This method assigns a separate GPFV to each covariate within a multivariate field while maintaining a constant structure across all covariates. The covariance function varies along the functional dimension based on a standard choice or user specification but remains constant across the longitudinal dimension. During GPFV fitting, the process is treated as if the data were one-dimensional, but post-processing involves smoothing the estimated covariance functions to accommodate the full dataset. We apply this approach to multivariate data on ocean currents from the North Atlantic, satellite temperature observations from NASA, the SPOT satellite, and a neural-style transfer learning dataset from Google. Our results demonstrate that estimates from the proposed method yield a better fit to the data and enhanced predictive accuracy compared to those from the `gpflow` and `GPflow` packages. The code is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/ahmadyalvar/multivariateGPVF. The `multivariate(GPFV)` package offers several multivariate GP models, currently supporting a linear model with an Mat\'ern 2.5 covariance function and an constant model with a Gaussian process spatial trend. Future versions will expand the library to include nonlinear models, such as Radial Basis Function and Splines, and introduce multiple realizations of the covariance function for each covariate. Furthermore, we plan to extend the method to handle dependencies within and between time points in temporal data, as well as between spatial coordinates in spatial data. The package is available via CRAN at: https://cran.r-project.org/package=multivariateGPVF.
