One strategy to address these limitations involves compiling quantum circuits into families of fixed-angle (frozen) circuits, optimized for maximum fidelity among all possible circuit structures within each family. We introduce a method to derive such frozen circuits for a broad range of single- and multi-qubit operations, capable of accounting for both unitary and non-unitary gate errors. Our approach yields highly accurate solutions for circuits with minimal depth and provides near-optimal results when scaled to greater depths, effectively adapting to specific hardware constraints. We apply this method to freeze general single-qubit gates within the NOISY-QNROM code family and to freeze multi-qubit T gates based on the T gates introduced by Knill. These techniques significantly reduce the number of multi-qubit operations, potentially boosting computational performance, and may also enhance measurement sensitivity in quantum interference experiments, including those related to gravitational searches. Furthermore, we outline a strategy for determining the optimal placement of multi-qubit gates during circuit compilation, aiming to maximize information extraction during intermediate algorithm measurements, a critical factor for hybrid quantum-classical approaches. Finally, we illustrate the utility of our methods through numerical simulations on a standard noise model for a single-qubit variant of Grover's algorithm. Our simulations indicate that these freezing approaches can improve computational accuracy for algorithms running on current quantum hardware, including emerging fault-tolerant systems.

Summary: We present a technique to mitigate quantum computational errors by reducing circuit depth through the substitution of arbitrary quantum gates with a small set of fixed-angle gates. This method generates highly precise frozen circuits for various tasks, tailored to specific computing hardware, and may offer substantial accuracy gains across diverse computational tasks. We demonstrate the method's utility in compiling arbitrary single- and multi-qubit operations into low-depth circuits utilizing a small basis of multi-qubit T gates and T\dag gates, compiled for NOISY-QNROM, a variant of the quantum circuit model incorporating non-unitary noise gates. Our simulation results show that these proposals can significantly boost computational accuracy on current noisy devices, a crucial step toward fault-tolerant computing. Additionally, we illustrate how to determine approximately optimal multi-qubit gate placements by analyzing frozen circuits, a consideration essential for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. We demonstrate that this placement strategy can achieve substantial improvements in computational accuracy on relevant quantum devices.

moiré heterostructures have created significant excitement within the condensed matter community. This paper offers a comprehensive review of mathematical physics principles in the context of two-dimensional materials and their moiré patterns. We begin by examining mathematical challenges in defining a two-dimensional material and offering a conceptual model for achieving a universal mathematical description. We then explore dimensionality-specific mathematical issues, including the reliance on global properties like symmetry, the role of local curvature, and topological considerations. Subsequently, we present a simplified "clay model" to illustrate a mathematically rigorous approach to describing moiré patterns in twisted bilayers. This is followed by an in-depth analysis of more complex scalar fields, gradient fields, and singularities inherent to moiré patterns. The review further connects these geometric structures to mathematical physics applications, such as elasticity theory for moiré patterns and differential equations in the CMS-Ginzburg-Landau framework. We conclude by highlighting open mathematical problems within this dynamic area of research. Writen as a lecture series, this work interweaves mathematical rigor with physical intuition to serve as a accessible entry point for physicists, engineers, and mathematicians. Key equations, laws, topological invariants, and other mathematical concepts are explicitly identified. Additionally, numerous references cover recent mathematical publications in this field, which are readily available to readers.

This survey addresses the classification of Fano manifolds through the lens of their homogeneous polynomial differential equations (hpde). Our primary finding is that the "moduli problem" for hpde is equivalent to the "moduli problem" for varieties admitting a non-trivial rational action by a reductive algebraic group, thereby establishing a correspondence between moduli spaces of hpde and moduli spaces of algebraic homogeneous varieties. We also provide a brief overview of the translation method between the two moduli problems. Subsequently, we present a novel application: characterizing all rank 1 polarized variation of Hodge structure moduli spaces, as well as the associated rigid singularities and their deformations, by translating the problem into the "moduli problem" for hpde. This approach leverages the rigorous nature of the latter to overcome limitations in existing literature. We note that a previous preprint titled "Malcev's Theorem and Polar Varieties" [arXiv:1912.00844] offered a similar proof. Finally, as a supplementary section, we outline a characterization of rank 1 hpde.

The analysis utilizes a dataset of $139$ fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $13$ TeV, recorded by the CMS detector at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. Candidate $W^{\pm}Z$ events are identified through the leptonic decays of these bosons into electrons and muons. For the first time, the simultaneous production of longitudinally polarized vector bosons is observed. The measured joint longitudinal joint longitudinal polarization probabilities are $P_{00}^{(\mu\nu)} = 0.173 \pm 0.021$ and $P_{00}^{(e\nu)} = 0.150 \pm 0.024$ for the $\mu+v$ and $e+v$ combinations, respectively. These results are compared with predictions from the Standard Model. Furthermore, a systematic search for the rare triple gauge boson coupling $WWB$ yields limits on its magnitude that improve upon existing constraints. Specifically, for an integrated luminosity of $139$ fb$^{-1}$, the 95% confidence level bounds on the coefficients $D_i$ (for $i=3,4$) are $\pm[0.3, 0.4]$ GeV$^{-1}$. These findings also translate into first-ever upper bounds on the triple gauge boson coupling parameters of the Left-Right symmetric model. Additionally, the data place a lower bound of $845$ GeV on the mass of the heavy $W$ boson $W^{'\pm}$. Finally, the study provides the first experimental restrictions on the parameters associated with the extension of the electroweak sector by a new heavy neutral vector boson $Z'$. Various sets of these model parameters are either excluded at the 95% confidence level or allowed with a p-value exceeding $0.05$.

Any solution to the Einstein equations, whether including or excluding a cosmological constant, adheres to the field equations defined by the Cotton tensor, indicating that the cosmological constant functions as an integration constant. In this theoretical framework, a vacuum state is characterized by the vanishing of the Cotton tensor instead of the Ricci tensor. Furthermore, an exact Schwarzschild-like solution for a static, spherically symmetric source has been identified. When a cosmological constant is incorporated, the field equations for the Cotton tensor yield the Kerr metric and the Schwarzschild–de Sitter solution. Additionally, a complex-valued exact solution representing a rotating black hole is presented as an exact solution to the field equations of the Cotton tensor. Finally, it is concluded that the Cotton tensor offers valuable insights into gravitational physics and holds promise as an alternative approach to gravitational field theory.

This construction applies a topology to Hartonas's elementary class of orthomodular frames, following Bimbó's adaptation of Goldblatt's representation theory for ortholattices. We subsequently demonstrate a dual equivalence between orthomodular lattices and their homomorphisms on one hand, and orthomodular spaces with their continuous frame morphisms on the other. This dual equivalence is mediated by the free orthomodular lattice functor applied to the underlying lattice functor of points. The study is directed by a Stone-type embedding that maps any orthomodular lattice into the dual space of its prime filter congruences, following Bimbó's approach. This specific instance of orthomodular space is a frame, and we provide a detailed analysis of its properties. Furthermore, we establish an equivalent category to spaces defined by Janssens's construction for representing orthomodular lattices, which is a subcategory of Kripke models. Our work also offers a novel perspective on identifying the precise conditions required of orthologic's dual structures—specifically, Herbrand's canonical frames—as defined by Bimbó, to ensure the validity of the principles of linearity and Duris's theorem. Additionally, we present a unitary modality within intuitionistic first-order logic that, via Kripke semantics, characterizes a first-order theory whose models are dual to subalgebras of the paraconsistent logic $N_4$. This paper introduces a new, efficient pre-conditioned Conjugate Gradient (CG) iterative solver designed to achieve a specified solution accuracy with a minimal number of iterations. By reducing the number of iterations, the method significantly lowers the total computational effort needed to optimize the solution. The pre-conditioning strategy utilizes the sparsity pattern of the constraint matrix, allowing the CG iterations to execute more rapidly than those of other solvers, typically resulting in fewer iterations per IPM iteration. Extensive numerical experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposed solver against other existing methods. The results demonstrate that the proposed pre-conditioned CG solver achieves lower solving times with fewer iterations compared to standard solvers for a specific accuracy threshold, and outperforms two leading solvers for another accuracy range. The pre-conditioned CG solver is implemented in C/C++, written in fewer than 1,000 lines, and is released as open-source under the MIT License, available at https://github.com/AliAslani1234/pcgsol. Every Unix system administrator knows that a missing dependency can bring a system to a halt; however, this issue is far more prevalent in modern software systems, which often fail silently due to incorrect AI model outputs. This paper presents a systematic investigation into daily AI system crashes occurring in submission systems for machine learning challenges. We examine crash types, frequencies, and rates, exploring factors such as submission volume, submission type, language, systems monitoring, and Linux distributions. Our analysis of 100,000 crashes across eight years reveals that security research is the primary cause (38.5%), followed by incorrect submissions (24.1%), import errors (11.5%), and Linux distribution issues (9.8%). These findings validate the significance of AI safety research in critical contexts like daily AI systems, edge computing, and autonomous vehicles. We share the data at https://anonymous(2024).ICML.org submission_crashes.

## 1 Introduction

In critical systems such as autonomous vehicles, every AI failure holds catastrophic consequences. Conversely, in non-critical settings like submission platforms for machine learning tasks, crash data is readily available and free to access. We posit that this data can aid in training failure detectors for AI safety or in building more robust AI systems. This paper presents a systematic study of AI crashes within submission systems for machine learning tasks.

Specifically, in scalar field theory, an exact link has been established between the gradient flow and the RG trajectory of the Wilson action within the exact renormalization group (ERG) framework. By emulating this relationship, we introduce an ERG differential equation for Yang–Mills theory that maintains explicit gauge invariance. Furthermore, our continuum formulation can be generalized to apply to lattice gauge theory. Using $SU(2)$ as a test case, we argue that the parameters of the continuum ERD accurately represent physical properties of lattice gauge theory in the continuum limit. Notably, even though the two theories differ at a finite scale, the discrepancy between their couplings is negligible for a fine flow parameter $b$, suggesting that the coupling derived from the gradient flow serves as an excellent approximation for the physical continuum coupling. This approach is particularly valuable because it naturally yields a gauge-invariant definition of the coupling, thereby circumventing the puzzles associated with the running of the Yang–Mills coupling. Finally, we outline a principle for defining the barometric flow on the lattice that becomes equivalent to the continuum flow in the continuum limit, enabling a precise determination of the non-perturbative beta function for lattice gauge theory. Our methodology is also applicable to $U(N)$ and $SU(N)$ theories as well as lattice Yang–Mills theories involving fundamental matter. (Article 8 pages)

However, certain scenarios necessitate the simultaneous consideration of multiple process specifications, which may be procedural, declarative, or hybrid. For instance, in healthcare, a clinical guideline for treating a specific disease might fail to capture every potential scenario, at no point violating any declarative rules, as long as no negative outcomes occur, or if negative outcomes arise, ensuring their proper management. This paper introduces a solution for monitoring the conjunction of multiple specifications, whether they are procedural, declarative, or hybrid. We present a method to generate a monitoring solution comprised of several concurrent finite-state machine (FSM) models. -dimensional percolation model characterized by a triangulated lattice where bonds are dimerized according to a control parameter that determines the density of self-intersecting triangles. This creates an interplay between percolation and frustration. This model serves as a simplified representation of graphene with randomly closed pentagonal defects. Our findings indicate that the model exhibits a reentrant phase transition: starting from the frustal triangle density as a parameter, the system transitions sequentially from a large percolating cluster phase to a frustrated percolation phase, and finally back to a percolating cluster phase. We analyze the critical behavior near the percolation point using finite-size scaling on large square tables with system sizes up to 100, applying standard percolation scaling analyses. We provide a scaling analysis of the percolation probability near the critical point using percolation exponents derived from finite-size scaling of relevant observables like percolation probability $P$ and cluster size susceptibility $\chi$. Furthermore, we examine the relationships between critical parameter values and other observable quantities, including the effective fractal dimension $d_f$, the percolation threshold $p_c$, the clustering coefficient $CC$, the percolation correlation length exponent $\nu$, and the upper critical dimension $d_U$. Our results demonstrate that the model retains long-range correlations up to table sizes as large as $L=100$, suggesting that the observed reentrant behavior is intrinsic to the model rather than an artifact of our analysis. For graphene, specific values of the pentagon parameter yield phase boundaries very close to those observed in real graphene samples. redundant and error-prone short reads is a critical yet computationally demanding phase in numerous genomics workflows. Wright's equation, was first formulated to account for oscillatory behaviors in ecological systems. Although it spurred the creation of numerous mathematical methods for analyzing nonlinear delay differential equations, it failed to achieve widespread adoption in actual ecological research. This limitation was primarily due to the infeasibility of the stepwise linear delay (SLD) feedback mechanism it required and the resulting difficulty this non-smoothness caused for mathematical analysis. In this work, we introduce a modified version of the stepwise linear delay feedback function that resolves these issues. While maintaining analysis feasibility, this adjustment enables the model to be implemented via a straightforward Euler-type numerical method. Using specific numerical examples, we demonstrate that this new model captures oscillatory dynamics consistent with biological observations and can be solved using an existing open-source software package. Furthermore, we show that our approach yields more accurate results compared to a previously used numerical technique for the original stepwise linear delay equation. Finally, we apply our model to a predator-prey system incorporating an insensitive functional response. The results indicate that the dynamics of this biologically more realistic model mirror those of the original stepwise linear delay logistic equation. The method developed here is broadly applicable to various delay equations in mathematical biology, including the aforementioned predator-prey model. ### I. INTRODUCTION

Quantum technologies are advancing at a rapid pace, with existing technologies now serving as a foundation for emerging ones. A prominent example is the quantum dot, a semiconductor nanostructure that acts as a confined electron box. These devices have been extensively utilized to build nanoscale energy converters, such as engines and heat pumps. Over the past fifteen years, significant progress has been made in quantum thermodynamics, the field of study of these miniaturized devices. Recent literature, including reviews and monographs, details the capabilities of quantum devices, the configuration of these thermal machines, and the specific quantum features that enhance their operational efficiency.

While the quantum enhancement of thermal machines remains an active area of research, our focus shifts to quantum uncertainty and fluctuation effects. These phenomena are particularly relevant for hybrid conductors, which we encounter frequently in quantum transport studies. A conductor is classified as hybrid when a quantum dot or similar orbital is connected to more than two leads connected to baths at distinct temperatures or chemical potentials. A common example involves a central quantum dot linked to an empty lead and a gated lead connected to a reservoir with a large electron density. These hybrid devices can convert energy derived from electronic chemical potentials into electric work and heat. Consequently, they serve as a natural framework for investigating high-efficiency multi-functional machines.

Concurrently, the deep learning community recognized that training increasingly complex models demands substantial energy, thereby contributing to GHG output. This study reviews recent literature to explore the circular relationship between deep learning and environmental sustainability, aiming to guide future research for the benefit of society. A systematic review was conducted on papers published between January 2011 and March 2021, sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library databases using specific keywords. After an initial pool of 200 papers, 73 were selected for analysis based on their relevance to both AI/specific techniques and environmental sustainability. The findings indicate a growing research interest in how deep learning impacts sustainability, with a significant increase in publications after 2019. The analyses highlight the dual role of deep learning in sustainability: as a driver of solutions through energy consumption studies and through the use of favorable hardware practices. However, the literature also reveals pitfalls, such as the heavy energy costs of cloud-based solutions. To address these issues, proposed strategies include utilizing renewable energy, optimizing algorithms, employing energy-efficient hardware, integrating hybrid methods, and selecting training locations powered by green energy. Ultimately, this paper aims to direct researchers toward specific techniques for more effective and environmentally responsible AI development. To illustrate these concepts, two examples—convolutional neural networks and federated learning—are provided to demonstrate practical applications in sustainable AI.

Recent research highlights that delays in RNA production associated with splicing can be substantial. We present a unified model integrating transcriptional activation and mRNA accumulation, designed to infer transcription rates, RNA production delays, and degradation rates using genome-wide data from high-throughput sequencing time courses. By merging a mechanistic differential equation framework with a non-parametric statistical approach, we accommodate diverse activation kinetics, prolonged mRNA plateau phases, and genomic-scale datasets with varying missing values. Applications to human HeLa cells (C644) and mouse ICF cells (C673) reveal a statistical association between transcriptional activation delays and mRNA half-lives, robustly predicted from activation kinetics. Specifically, in the ICF dataset, an positive correlation is observed as anticipated, since ICF cells lack functional deadenylation. Additionally, we examine the impact of transcriptional delays on noisy, intermittent transcription and explore methodologies for estimating stochastic transcription rates. While our approach validates distinct transcriptional profiles across species, the techniques for quantifying delay distributions and decay rates are broadly applicable to any high-quality time-course mRNA data. We have made these methods publicly available via the delays R package. Furthermore, ongoing collaborations with laboratory colleagues to generate new high-quality time-series data will be ongoing. This study examines how public sector officials evaluate their reliance on Google, their awareness of algorithmic biases affecting information retrieval, and the extent of relevant data potentially lost due to personalization. Our experimental results reveal that most participants are unaware of these risks. This review introduces a novel class of graph-based algorithms designed to detect hidden symmetries in conservative mechanical systems. The optical and near-infrared follow-up of the resulting kilonova—the ejected material from such mergers—provided the first evidence that heavy nuclei are synthesized via the rapid neutron capture process (r-process) in these astrophysical environments. Since the emission characteristics of a kilonova are heavily influenced by the opacities of the ejected matter, there has been a recent drive to improve the limited available atomic data for the r-process. Despite this motivation, the intricate electronic structures of these heavy elements necessitate significant further effort to achieve reliable atomic data. This study aims to address this gap for low-charge-state elements within the osmium-like isoelectronic sequence. Utilizing the general-purpose relativistic atomic structure codes GRASP0 and GRASP2K, we calculated energy levels and transition probabilities (E1 and M1), providing line lists and expansion opacities for various r-process elements. Our focus centers on the Os isoelectronic sequence (Os I, Ir II, Pt III, Au IV, Hg V). We benchmark our findings against existing experimental data and previous calculations, offering predictions for kilonova emission spectra. Additionally, we highlight infrared fine-structure (M1) lines that may be observable by the James Webb Space Telescope. Finally, we discuss our findings in the context of resolving current discrepancies regarding opacities. Line lists are accessible at \url{http://www.astro.su.se/~atomic/kilonova/}.

By utilizing MR-Linacs, which combine magnetic resonance imaging with linear accelerators, oncologists can visualize tumor positions in real-time and deliver precise radiation doses that account for daily variations in tumor cell presence. Currently, manually outlining the stomach and intestines to adjust beam directions for safe dose delivery is a time-consuming and labor-intensive task. This process often extends daily treatment times from 15 minutes to an hour because organs move with their natural contents; for instance, an empty stomach may suddenly fill with liquid, causing it to shift and necessitating manual observation and beam direction re-outlining. This manual interplay between tumor organ motion and physician decisions, alongside the actual tumor exposure, constitutes a Markov Decision Process (MDP). In this study, we introduce LineOfSight, a system that uses deep reinforcement learning and the Monte Carlo method to suggest optimal beam directions that avoid shifting organs, potentially extending patient treatment time by an additional 10 minutes per session. Our results demonstrate that the system reduces tumor exposure to stomach and intestinal movements by 50% while maintaining a 10% margin of error. These findings indicate that deep reinforcement learning can help increase the dose received by tumors during cancer ray treatment. Both the challenges and solutions presented here offer a novel contribution to both artificial intelligence and radiology. Our code and models are accessible at https://github.com/LineOfSight-MRL/RL-outlining. The line-of-sight algorithm demonstrates a 50% reduction in tumor radiation, achieving an average score of 85.

. A key challenge is determining how an artificial attention model can simultaneously identify relevant stimuli and execute tasks. Addressing this, we introduce a novel training approach for learnable and configurable sub-nuclear branch filters within a ball-and-rod based artificial brain. Through experiments on a two-task environment, we demonstrate that a global attention model relying solely on a single branch type fails to solve both tasks. Their primary function is to utilize data point histories to anticipate future points via time-based prediction (TBP) functions, a method applicable to diverse scenarios such as stock price forecasting, weather prediction, and anomaly detection. Addressing this challenge, we introduce TCube, a novel framework designed to generate temporal narratives for time-series data without requiring manual features. (LHC) has conducted precise measurements of mixing and CP violation in neutral B mesons, as well as rare processes in electroweak FCNC-suppressed neutral B-meson decays. This contribution highlights the most recent ATLAS findings, specifically the measurements of rare decays $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$, along with the determination of CP violation in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. These rare decay measurements employ a simultaneous analysis of the decays $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$, combined with world-average inputs, which constrain two key parameters in the FCNC sector of the Standard Model: the CKM-related parameter $|V_{tb}v_{ts}|$ and the Wilson coefficient $C_{tt}$. Furthermore, the simultaneous measurement of CP violation in the $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$ decay, performed across seven decay time intervals, provides a precise determination of the CP-violating angle $\Phi_s$, while also setting a limit on the CP asymmetry parameter $\alpha_s$. The ATLAS results for $\Phi_s$ and $C_{tt}$ are in agreement with corresponding measurements from the LHCb and LHCb+ALICE experiments. Additionally, the current ATLAS limit on the branching ratio $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-)$ aligns with other LHC experiments. When combined with the LHCb and LHCX world averages and projected limits, these findings offer a valuable dataset for tests of the FCNC sector within the Standard Model and a benchmark for various new physics models. Furthermore, an improved measurement of the branching ratio $\mathcal{B}(B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-)$ is achievable through a similar approach. Additionally, a search for a second CP-violating phase in the FCNC-suppressed decays $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ has been conducted by ATLAS. The latest results are consistent with the Standard Model prediction of one CP-violating phase derived from weak charged-current interactions. These new results serve as a benchmark for subsequent searches for new physics in the FCNC sector. Finally, a summary of LHC-b and LHCX world contributions to flavor physics is provided. artificial intelligence paradigm capable of training models to perform complex tasks, even when explicit rules are difficult to define. Yet, this approach demands extensive data and computational resources, facing significant challenges in generalizing to new inputs. Transfer learning helps address this by leveraging data from one domain to improve performance in another, Lifting RL takes this a step further by generalizing to new tasks, and integrating transfer learning with RL has yielded remarkable outcomes, such as an AI that mastered the game of Go. This paper introduces a new system that merges deep reinforcement learning with simulated annealing (SA) to solve combinatorial optimization problems (COPs), specifically the graph coloring problem (GCP). Given a graph where nodes represent items (like students) and edges indicate constraints, the goal is to ensure connected nodes are assigned different values, such that no two connected items share the same class. We trained a deep RL agent on the GCP, adapted it using transfer learning, and applied it to solve the GCP across various instances. Additionally, we integrated simulated annealing into this framework to create a lifted reinforcement learning system with simulated annealing (LSA). Our findings demonstrate that both the transfer learning and LSA approaches outperform both deep RL and SA when handling larger, more complex graph instances. ANNs) have led the field in computer vision, audio recognition, and natural language processing, driving widespread adoption across major global technology firms. However, the massive computational and energy demands required for training and deploying ANNs have historically hindered their large-scale implementation. Concurrently, neuromorphic computing platforms have emerged as a promising alternative, successfully executing bio-realistic Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with high throughput and minimal power usage. SNNs mimic biological neurons and synapses by utilizing "spikes"—discrete events signaling neuronal firing—making them well-suited for processing natural event-driven data. This paper presents an experimental evaluation of SNNs for speech activity detection, the capability to identify speaking periods within audio streams. Our results demonstrate that SNNs effectively compete with ANNs while offering superior energy and computational efficiency. By leveraging the event-based nature of SNNs, speech activity detection can be realized through off-line processing of pre-recorded audio or real-time detection of live speech. Our experiments focused on the latter, implementing an real-time speech activity detector using LIF neurons on a Kimera neuromorphic processor, compared against the same task performed with ReLU/GRU layers on a GPU. We found that the SNN-based detector achieved reasonable detection accuracy with significantly higher efficiency. Furthermore, we explored the effects of increasing neuron parameters (such as the number of neurons and synapses) in SNNs to determine if performance could be enhanced without compromising energy efficiency. Our experiments reveal that the number of synapses per neuron is the critical parameter for optimizing both efficiency and performance. It is also plausible that the spiking dynamics of LIF neurons, compared to GRUs, inherently contribute to the observed gains in efficiency and adequate accuracy. This research establishes a new benchmark for speech activity detection using SNNs, marking the first experimental investigation into speech activity detection utilizing live user input on a neuromorphic processor. Additionally, it sets a new precedent for competing with ANN-based systems in specific applications where ANNs offer substantial advantages over SNNs. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the most fundamental experimental comparison between ANNs and SNNs for speech activity detection on actual hardware, implemented at scale with live user input. We believe this experimental setup will inspire future comparative studies between these two computing paradigms in speech technology and beyond. The implementation code will be made available publicly upon completion of this work. Finally, we hope this paper will encourage further research into SNN applications within the speech technology community.

Specifically, it extracts privacy-sensitive attributes from CDMA 1x EV-DO wireless base station optimization messages. These attributes include the identity type (user or system), identification method, location data, and subscription details. Furthermore, the signaling intelligence matrix is utilized to detect privacy leaks. Experimental results demonstrate that the user identity classification model achieves a high accuracy rate of 93%, while the identification method classification model reaches an accuracy of 85%. Additionally, the leak detection model exhibits a high accuracy rate of 83%. Finally, the effectiveness of this signaling intelligence threat intelligence framework is evaluated through various use cases. This approach not only enhances awareness among wireless network operators and equipment vendors regarding potential privacy threats but also equips privacy protection experts and regulators with the necessary tools to mitigate risks. The methodology is applicable to other wireless access technologies, such as LTE and 5G NR, though specific attributes and models would need to be adjusted accordingly. This study introduces a novel feature-based ensemble learning framework tailored for efficient training and scaling. The method is built upon the principle that the training process of any feature-based ensemble model consists of two fundamental components: (i) feature selection, which determines the split features at each node, and (ii) vote counting, which involves training bags of examples to perform vote counting across different nodes. Specifically, we propose that feature selection and vote counting are independent tasks; consequently, they can be executed concurrently. This parallel execution is achievable by implementing feature selection and vote counting as separate threads within a single program. As a proof of concept, we applied our method to train random forests, where we successfully achieved a substantial reduction in training time relative to the conventional sequential approach. However, the exchange of these parameters creates a new vulnerability: while private data remains secure, the learned parameters can be reverse-engineered to reveal sensitive information. Current detection methods rely on statistical tests of global parameters, which are inefficient in federated environments. This work introduces a decentralized anomaly detection mechanism for federated deep learning that operates without the need for global parameters, safeguarding both parties' local information. During runtime, Timeloops identifies which system calls a program should execute while blocking unauthorized attempts. It overcomes several limitations of current static analysis approaches, such as the overly permissive soundsness found in containerless microservice setups, the high overhead of dynamic baselineing methods, and the complexity of crafting complex logic in proxy-based solutions. The system derives its filtering policy from multiple execution histories, consolidates these into a compact representation, and utilizes time-sensitive, recurrent neural networks to classify system calls as authorized or unauthorized. Empirical results on Google's Microservice Benchmark demonstrate that Timeloops systems reject 90% of malicious system calls with less than a 0.1% false positive rate, achieving less than 1% system-level overhead. We conclude by discussing the practical benefits of Timeloops for microservice development and providing a characterization of its empirical behavior. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/Timeloops.

Our empirical evaluation reveals that the system's performance is primarily determined by two factors: the sampling interval and the training procedure. The sampling interval impacts both runtime latency and accuracy, whereas the training process is essential for achieving precise classification. Our empirical analysis indicates that the most efficient configuration involves a sampling interval of less than one second and approximately one hour of training time. Additionally, we observe that the system's scale does not influence its efficiency. At the extremums of our empirical search space, the fastest configuration uses a sampling interval of one second, one hour of training time, and yields a forward pass latency of 0.2 -- 0.4 milliseconds. Given these characteristics, Timeloops offers the potential for practical deployment to enhance the security of microservice development. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic investigation into the systematic, precision, and scalability of System Call Control for microservice environments. This work tackles the emerging challenge of linear classification within product space forms, specifically those combining Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic geometries. First, we introduce the Conceptual Product Space (CPS) as a novel mathematical framework for geometric machine learning. Second, we develop new embedding strategies for product space manifolds suitable for classification tasks. Finally, utilizing recent advances in geometric machine learning, we demonstrate the utility of CPS-manifold classifiers through application to hierarchical classification of CMS 11.5D categorical data. The hierarchical structure of this dataset naturally forms a hyperbolic-spherical product space manifold, defined by the duality of its CMS 11 categories: eight hierarchies are hyperbolic, while the remaining seven are spherical. Our findings indicate that even a rudimentary CPS embedding, combined with logistic regression, yields 95.4% correct classifications. We anticipate these results to serve as a foundation for future research on hierarchical classification in product space geometries.

Furthermore, this approach permits the determination of the quasi-hydrodynamic structure of stars in the immediate vicinity of $M_{\bullet}$ and, when compared with high-precision observational data, constrains the dynamical evolution of the surrounding stellar population.

This paper examines the Independent Component Analysis (ICA) framework through the lens of compressive learning. Specifically, we demonstrate that solutions derived from the cumulant-based ICA model exhibit a specific structure, forming a low-dimensional set within the cumulant tensor space. By establishing that random cumulants, such as Gaussians or Rademacher variables, also satisfy this structure, we present efficient algorithms for identifying these structures in both compressive and non-compressive learning settings. These methods significantly reduce the storage requirements for the cumulant tensor. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm capable of extracting multiple structure types simultaneously within a low-rank tensor. We illustrate how this approach can be applied to uncover structure types in both real and complex tensors. Most importantly, we show how leveraging these structures can enhance the performance of compressive ICA. Numerical experiments validate that integrating the proposed method with existing algorithms successfully recovers independent signals from their mixed versions, even under adverse conditions characterized by low sampling rates and heavy noise. These findings confirm the effectiveness of our method in various scenarios, including signal mixing coefficients with two non-zero values, arbitrary mixing coefficients, and cases where the number of observations is less than the number of mixed signals. Our approach shows greater robustness compared to COMBp and HOGPIG methods; notably, our method can achieve successful recovery with a sampling rate as low as 0.25, whereas COMBp requires a rate approximately 1.33 times higher to ensure successful recovery.

In this system, one species can immigrate from external sources, whereas the other species lacks this capability but possesses higher dispersal rates. This tradeoff implies that the species with the immigration advantage possesses a dispersal disadvantage, meaning a larger proportion of its population consists of non-reproductive dispersers. Through analytical methods, we identified the conditions under which both coexistence and invision—where one species drives the other to extinction)—can occur. Specifically, both outcomes emerge from a bifurcation occurring at a critical threshold for both the immigration rate and the dispersal cost. Numerical simulations based on both symmetric and asymmetric scenarios confirm these theoretical predictions. Our findings indicate that coexistence is more likely when the immigrating species has the lower dispersal cost, and that immigration-dispersal tradeoffs can sustain coexistence even when immigration is intense. Overall, these results highlight that immigration interactions can have complex effects on competitive dynamics, potentially preventing species loss and enabling the persistence of multiple species.

The parton shower (PS) framework remains a critical link between high-energy theoretical predictions and experimental data. Its significance is heightened as next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) calculations introduce a parton-level complexity unlike any previous fixed-order computations. This paper introduces a Monte Carlo algorithm for parton evolution that maintains a specific color configuration of the final state. We verify the shower's correctness at next-to-leading order (NLO) by calculating NLO corrections for specific PS regions, specifically $qg \to qg$ and $q\bar{q} \to \tau^+\tau^-$ across two distinct PS settings. Since the region where the PS is valid differs between these two showers, our per-region NLO checks provide a comprehensive validation of the entire algorithm's correctness. We provide proofs for two analogous results required to establish the correctness of the proposed PS algorithm. First, we extend a well-known theorem to $2 \to 3$ processes: if a $2 \to 2$ amplitude is color-ordered such that the squared amplitude factorizes correctly upon attaching a gluon, then the resulting squared amplitude for the $2 \to 3$ process also factorizes correctly upon attaching a fourth gluon. Second, we prove a associated lemma. Furthermore, we generalize an existing lemma to $2 \to 3$ processes. These results, which were vital in proving the correctness of a previous angular-ordered PS, are relevant to our new PS formulation because many of our generalized proofs follow the same logical structure.

This paper examines spectra for sentences involving a bounded number of variables and relations, focusing particularly on those with at most three variables. We introduce and analyze the spectra of sentences with a limited number of variables that exclude losing models—characterized by the absence of a single element participating in an bounded number of relational instances. We demonstrate that such spectra are effectively descriptive, meaning they can be expressed using first-order logic with a single new relation symbol where the original structure serves as an model. Furthermore, we show that when the lossless fraction—the ratio of winning elements to the total element count—approaches one, the spectra of three-variable sentences with a bounded number of relations are also effectively descriptive. In contrast, for sentences with three variables and a fixed lossless fraction strictly between zero and one, we prove that their spectra are effectively computable but generally not descriptive, although specific fractions yield effectively descriptive scenarios. Finally, we outline an algorithm to transform any finite set of models into a single model representing their common type, thereby clarifying the relationship between the undecidability of spectra and the theory of sentences with a bounded number of variables. As an supplementary analysis, we detail the complexity of deciding spectra for these sentences.

This study derives a semi-analytical formula for the dynamical density-density linear-response function (the "Lindhard" function) of noninteracting massless Dirac fermions at finite temperatures. This result is essential for characterizing the finite-temperature screening of interacting massless Dirac fermions within the Random Phase Approximation. Specifically, we utilize this formula to generate quantitative predictions for the specific heat and compressibility of doped graphene sheets. Our findings indicate that at low temperatures, the specific heat exhibits the standard linear-in-temperature behavior typical of a normal Fermi liquid, with the slope determined exclusively by the renormalized quasiparticle velocity. Furthermore, the relative corrections to the Fermi-liquid predictions for both specific heat and compressibility are directly proportional to the square of the interaction coupling constant. These insights enable the quantitative analysis of low-temperature thermodynamic properties in doped graphene. Additionally, we note that the same formula applies to a recently proposed "chiral" fermion lattice model. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for future experiments involving massless Dirac fermions in other condensed-matter systems, such as semiconductor quantum wells with extreme parabolicity and multiple Weyl nodes in Weyl semimetals. Our findings also have relevance for photonic crystals supporting Dirac cones. Furthermore, our work provides a quantitative benchmark for recent numerical simulations. These massless Dirac fermions, observed in graphene, represent a unique class of low-energy quasiparticles, prompting pertinent questions in field and particle physics regarding the existence of free massless Dirac fermions at finite temperatures. Specifically, no such fermions have been observed in nuclear or particle physics, a fact that we elucidate in relation to the thermodynamic properties calculated here. This work establishes a unique link between the standard model of particle physics and theoretical condensed-matter physics. Indeed, the specific heat of a normal Fermi liquid consists of a velocity term and a temperature-term correction; we show that for massless Dirac fermions, this correction is negligible, explaining why it has never been detected experimentally. We anticipate that this theoretical understanding of the low-temperature thermodynamics of Dirac fermions will prove valuable to researchers in multiple fields. Indeed, our formulas represent an exact solution to the spinless sine-Gordon model in two dimensions in the free-charge sector. This capability enables the calculation of the spin-wave stiffness for spin waves arising from nearly-charged interacting Dirac fermions in

This study investigates (1) whether DNNs encounter similar vulnerabilities when trained on noisy data and (2) if certain input features are consistently more critical for accurate classification. To address these questions, we employ (a) adversarial training, which exposes models to adversarial samples during the training phase, and (b) a novel method called "random projection," which reduces input dimensionality randomly. The KMZ approach leverages a type-closed subgroup, such as one defined by gender, to isolate an immutable characteristic, namely English competence, using a difference-in-differences framework. We argue that their claimed finding — that "English competence acquired in utero raises lifetime wages" — rests on two critical assumptions that are difficult to verify: first, that immigrants' English skills are at par with those of non-immigrants; and second, that this language competence remains constant across all destinations, including the distinction between English- and non-English-speaking regions. These assumptions are inherently unverifiable. Consequently, by relying on an ad-hoc cohort selection rather than a random assignment mechanism, the KMZ method may produce upward bias in estimated wage effects for high English-speaking environments and downward bias for others, ultimately masking the true impact of English language skills. Consequently, we contend that the fundamental goal of explaining the Norwegian Puzzle may not have been achieved. To offer an alternative perspective that does not require type-closed subgroups and is not hindered by unverifiable assumptions, we apply a Bayesian Bayesian Reduced Form (BBR) approach within a broader wage regression discontinuity framework. This method evaluates the causal impact of the shock on English competence — measured as the shift in the wage distribution caused by the location change — on lifetime wages. In this framework, the causal effect of the 1969 location shift corresponds to the difference between the "pre-born" wage distribution before the shock and the "post-born" distribution after 1969. Our findings reject the null hypothesis that English competence had no effect (p-value = 0.03). Moreover, contrary to the upward bias suggested by KMZ, our analysis indicates that post-born immigrants may actually exhibit lower English competence than their pre-born counterparts. Finally, we provide insight into the causal mechanism, interpreting the puzzle through a "compound effect" of multiple Causal Intermediate Treatment Effects (CITEs), where "low English competence" acts as a common cause increasing productivity in both English-speaking and non-English-speaking cities. This work introduces a conceptual design for a unified scattering facility that accelerates electrons, protons, ions, and neutrinos to study a single target. The proposed scheme leverages a linear accelerator (linac) supported by an electromagnetic RF field to drive all particle beams. By arranging collision points within an extended target region, the facility allows scattering experiments using multiple beam types to occur at one location. Given the versatility of such a facility, it could serve as a valuable shared research infrastructure for the high-energy physics and nuclear physics communities at major research centers. The concept is referred to as the Multi-Messenger Scattering Research Accelerator (MMSRA).

**I. INTRODUCTION** The gravitational constant $G$ is notoriously difficult to measure with high precision, as its extremely small magnitude demands exceptionally sensitive experimental techniques. Historically, experiments determining $G$ have faced challenges regarding reproducibility, with different studies often yielding disparate results. To address this, international collaborations have formed the Weight of the Universe ($G$) collaboration, aiming to measure $G$ with greater accuracy and subject the measurement to a rigorous, transparent experimental protocol. This mobility is essential for the experiment because sensitivity tests involve placing a spherical gravitational source near a torsion balance within a vacuum chamber. Given the minute nature of the gravitational force, the experiment must also minimize unwanted perturbations from other forces to avoid masking the weak gravitational signal. Furthermore, the experimental setup needs to accommodate students of varying age groups within a limited classroom area. The mobile gravitational source functions as a spherical mass suspended from a steel rod; by adjusting the rod's position, the force applied to the balance changes. To validate the mobile source's impact on the torsion balance, we conducted a simplified experiment using a sodium MOT. We compared results from a standard $436$ nm MOT configuration against one where the trap was positioned $10$ cm closer to the balance cup. This study confirms that the mobile module does not exert any significant perturbation on the torsion balance. Additionally, we addressed the spatial constraint challenge by reducing the overall system dimensions to under $50 \times 50$ cm$^2$, making it an ideal fit for small teaching rooms. Finally, we discuss the trade-offs between further miniaturization and MOT performance.

Recent observations of young, massive stellar candidates showing no evidence of mass accretion processes suggest that massive stars may indeed be born with large masses. Nevertheless, the intense radiation from these stars creates a radiation pressure barrier—similar to the Hayashi or decretion limits in lower-mass star formation—potentially restricting the mass-assembly phase. Biometric authentication has gained prominence in recent years due to the increasing volume of sensitive data held by organizations. This authentication method verifies user identity using unique biological traits. However, document-based authentication methods remain prevalent in certain sectors due to their cost-effectiveness and convenience. Despite this, both biometric and document-based authentication approaches are vulnerable to forgery attempts by malicious users. Consequently, organizations have adopted multi-factor authentication (MFA), which integrates multiple authentication types to enhance security. This thesis presents a hybrid authentication system combining document-based and biometric methods for organization security. The system validates an individual's identity through three factors: an ID card image, an passport photo, and live facial recognition. The algorithm compares input card images with stored database entries using a modified template matching technique that supports multior scale range operations. Simultaneously, the authentication process compares the user's face against their stored biometric template. The final decision grants or denies access by combining the outcomes from both authentication methods. This research was conducted on two document datasets: the Indian Smart Card and the South African ID card. Experiments were performed on the South African ID card dataset with variations in image parameters to assess performance under different conditions. Evaluation metrics included precision, recall, F1-score, and accuracy, with additional analysis of false acceptance and false rejection rates. Experiments were also conducted on the Indian Smart Card dataset, though specific results were not provided. The proposed method achieved approximately 97% accuracy, an 11% improvement over existing methods. Furthermore, the system exhibits reduced computational complexity compared to other techniques.

along the boundary of dual electromagnetic metasurfaces that maintain mirror reflection symmetry. Prior theoretical and experimental investigations have identified these waves in microwave and terahertz frequency ranges, demonstrating their emergence through a symmetric resistance transition from negative to positive values combined with uniform surface reactance. These waves exhibit tunable confinement, polarization dependent on incident direction, and mode scaling laws. This study introduces Poincaré line waves as an extended mode within a pair of chiral metasurfaces located along a closed line path. They arise when the effective surface resistance transitions from imaginary to real values and when the reactive component of the surface impedance for Poincaré spheres oriented north-south differs from that of oppositely oriented spheres by a sign. The authors present a complete set of design guidelines for achieving these waves in a meta-ribbon configuration. These lines are also predicted to appear in a triangular loop configuration, a scenario where threefold rotational symmetry forces the lack of polarization splitting upon incidence. Both microwave and terahertz experimental setups confirm the confinement of these modes, with a reported minimum mode wavelength of 0.7 times the incident wavelength. Like their counterparts as circular and flatline waves, Poincaré line waves offer significant potential for applications in advanced imaging and sensing systems. Furthermore, this work establishes a general methodology for generating new line wave modes in lossless chiral metasurfaces. This approach can be adapted to produce other polarization-confined line waves, such as topological line waves and Dirac line waves. Ultimately, this research provides another pathway for line wave discovery, advancing the field of meta-optics and related sub-disciplines within electromagnetic metasurfaces. Additionally, these findings contribute to the broader study of singular modes in other mathematical areas, including Laplacian and Helmholtz operators on manifolds and graphs. These singular modes are increasingly recognized for their utility in advanced meta-optical designs. The accompanying supplementary material offers a comprehensive derivation and explanation of the line wave singularities in cholic functions on a two-sphere, which corresponds to the effective impedance surface behavior on a plane. Twitter serves as a significant source of public sentiment. However, the platform's inherent openness allows anyone to publish any content, resulting in a high volume of irrelevant posts that complicate sentiment analysis. This study evaluates the efficacy of filtering Twitter data related to the COVID-19 vaccine before analyzing public opinion. We compare sentiment scores with and without preprocessing, which eliminates spam, bots, duplicate, and irrelevant tweets. This paper examines the removal of redundant information from Twitter data concerning vaccines and COVID social media discourse. Specifically, the removal of redundant tweets enhanced the F1 score by 10.2% for negative sentiment and by 4.5% for positive sentiment. However, in social media, user activities often lack precise spatial or temporal details. Specifically, users may share check-ins with imprecise locations, such as "beach," "city center," or "airport," alongside status updates. These activities might align in time for some users but not others. Consequently, social media stream mining for spatio-temporal density anomalies presents a distinct challenge: it must account for both the imprecision in user activities and the variation in the number of social media social media participants across different events. To address this, we introduce a framework for anomalous activity and eventuality detection in social media streams. This framework estimates spatio-temporal density based on the variation in user activity variation participation over specific locations and time intervals. We defined two types of events for this framework: "definite events," characterized by users providing events with check-ins with precise locations, and "probabilistic events," characterized by users sharing status updates without check-ins. To evaluate the effectiveness of this framework in detecting anomalous activities, we designed a detector with two associated parameters, the First Order Parameter (FOP) and the Second Order Parameter (SOP), which identify anomalies by comparing local densities with user activity participation in regions and time intervals. Experiments were conducted using social media stream datasets containing injected anomalies. Our findings show that the ANODE framework can successfully detect up to 85% of spatio-temporal density anomalies in social media streams. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ANODE can effectively predictprobabilistic events. These results suggest that the proposed framework and its parameters offer a promising approach for anomalous activity and eventuality detection in social media streams. Additionally, the FOP and SOP parameters can be tuned to be event-centric or interest group-based, enabling the discovery of anomalies related to natural disasters, disasters, or gatherings. Neural architecture search (NAS) has gained traction as a prominent method for autonomously generating optimal network structures for specific tasks; however, most existing NAS approaches focus narrowly on minimizing parameters without adequately addressing computation complexity. the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a potential lack of consideration for the loss function's impact. This paper investigates whether the type of loss function acts as a sensitive factor during the training of supervised classifiers. Our empirical analysis examines the performance of 154 distinct loss functions. Drawing on the observation that many losses differ primarily through their differentiable operators, we evaluated the sensitivity of each loss function to backpropagation methods, also testing sensitivity to stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates. Our experimental framework combines a black-box approach, which screens through a diverse set of losses to measure performance, with a white-box approach, which rationalizes these results by analyzing the loss landscape in conjunction with different differentiation strategies and datasets. Our findings indicate that selecting a loss function is highly dataset-dependent, and that the sensitivity of this selection is significantly influenced by the employed backpropagation method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reasoning is intuitive when utilizing the white-box approach to differentiate between training scenarios. Ultimately, our results confirm that the choice of loss function is a factor that can potentially lead to substantial performance gains. Consequently, we propose extending hyperparameter search protocols to investigate promising loss functions alongside other critical parameters, thereby enabling improved selector mechanisms that account for dependencies among various hyperparameters. We have made all experimental components, including our extensive collection of loss functions, available in an open-access repository. This work serves as a stepping stone toward smarter, more effective, and highly performant loss function selectors. The repository can be found at https://github.com/DistIL/distance-based-loss-functions. correlations within assemblies of strongly interacting particles, where quantum correlations play a pivotal role. This work presents an introduction to quasispecies representations of interacting bosons. Within this framework, a new kind of "single-particle" state emerges from the perspective of a Wigner configuration space, spatially centered on a specific position. These states are constructed to respect both the symmetry requirements of Hilbert spaces and the metric of configuration space. Consequently, they form a resolution of the identity in Wigner space that adheres to a positive metric, enabling the development of a "single-particle" Schrödinger equation. To achieve this, we utilize a recently created basis in quasispace that is both creation-unitary and complete. This basis partitions the many-particle Hilbert space into a physically significant "low-energy" subspace and a rapidly varying remainder, with the latter structured as a creation-space. We provide an introduction to quasispecies and their associated creation-space, followed by a formulation of the resolution of the identity in Wigner space and the "single-particle" Schrödinger equation. Finally, we derive a Riesz representation for quasispecies and explore its implications for quasispace metrics. To validate these concepts, we apply them to models of explicitly solvable interacting bosons. To demonstrate their practical utility, we establish a phase-space representation of quasispecies and establish a link to the phase-cutoff approximation, a widely used method for addressing interacting bosons. This establishes creation-space as a tool for generating effective field theories suitable for physical applications. To render this abstract formulation more tangible, we provide a simple geometric interpretation of quasispecies, illustrated by explicit quasispecies representations for Gaussian many-particle wave functions. To complete our introduction, we also include a brief review of creation-space formulated as a Krein space. We conclude that quasispecies representations offer valuable insights into the fundamental nature of boson collective phenomena. Furthermore, they facilitate a effective-field theory description of these effects, focusing on long-wavelength dynamics and large quantum fluctuations. Additionally, quasispace and its associated creation-space introduce a meta-space, from which one can derive even simpler representations of quasispace and establish a mapping between it and creation-space.

For a system containing $V$ noninteracting particles, the number of particles that can be spontaneously transformed into condensate excitations scales as $V^{1-\epsilon}$, where $\epsilon$ follows a Cauchy distribution with a distribution width of $1/V$. Our analysis indicates that the critical phenomena in 2D noninter Bose systems differ significantly from those in 3D. To enhance the accuracy of automatic incident classification, it is crucial to understand the semantic relationships among different categories of incidents; however, researching these relationships demands a robust classification framework. Although supervised learning methods have been extensively applied in previous research, their performance is generally limited by dependency on large datasets and the failure to account for the community-specific nature of incident semantics. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging the power of few-shot learning to improve category definitions with minimal examples while simultaneously capturing community-driven semantic nuances to boost classification precision. By utilizing the Computational Ludics framework, we unify these two principles into a single condition termed the harmony condition. This reformulation elucidates two core intuitions: the concept of "containment" inherent in the inversion principle, and the notion that the recovery principle serves as the "converse" of inversion. Furthermore, we define two additional conditions within the Computational Ludics framework and demonstrate that each is equivalent to the harmony condition. Specifically, one of these new conditions generalizes the standard formulation of the recovery principle found in existing research. We also establish that the other new condition, the avoidance condition, is equivalent to the traditional recovery principle under the Computational Ludics framework. Consequently, the distinction between avoidance and recovery becomes clear: recovery represents an "active" principle, whereas avoidance is "passive." Finally, we demonstrate that both the equivalence condition and the exclusion condition are likewise equivalent to the harmony condition. This allows us to characterize computational traits through two principles: a computational condition and a metacomputational condition. The computational condition serves as the "principle," while the equivalence or exclusion condition indicates whether a trait is "constructive" or "non-constructive." For instance, the first-order existence predicate is existential, the exclusion-free implication is constructive, and the totality predicate is non-constructive. However, the bi-conditional is not an exclusion principle; thus, quantifying over it is non-computational, while substituting it is computational. Similarly, the non-contradiction predicate is non-computational, while the falsum and bottom are computational. The key insight driving this research is that Computational Ludics allows multiple perspectives on the same phenomenon. By contrasting proof-theoretic semantics, which separates linguistic rules from validity conditions into two distinct principles, Computational Ludics unifies them into a single validity condition known as the harmony condition. This provides an alternative characterization of computational traits that clarifies the role of the "inversion principle," distinguishing between active/reconstructive and passive avoidance, and offers an alternative understanding of the "validity condition," differentiating between constructive and non-constructive, and distinguishing between properties that are decidable and merely existential. The exclusion condition functions as the "first-order condition," while the harmony condition encompasses the "second-order condition." The equivalence condition establishes a connection between first-order and second-order reasoning. The abandonment condition categorizes traits as practical or theoretical

Given concerns about unknown or incorrect treatment models, researchers often adopt randomization tests for hypothesis testing because they only require the assumption of treatment non-interference. We propose a approach where the attention remains on the original model's validity rather than relying on randomization, leveraging instead the law of large numbers inherent in AIPW estimation. Our primary contribution is establishing the attitude toward either the original model or the AIPW estimator within the context of double machine learning. Specifically, we demonstrate that attention can be directed toward the treated model even when using an AIPW estimator for ATE estimation for double machine learning models. Two examples illustrate these findings: multiple linear regression and deep learning. Empirical evidence suggests that the deep learning example yields better performance than the original model, even when the original model is a multiple linear regression. Additionally, we provide convergence rate results and test validity results that support attention being placed on the original model. Finally, we address a common misconception regarding AIPW usage and offer guidelines for researchers when selecting between AIPW and other ATE estimators.

This simple experimental setup, which mirrors the fundamental dynamics of Earth's rotating atmosphere, enables the direct study of baroclinic instability. In this system, heat is applied radially across the annulus walls while the entire apparatus rotates at a constant angular velocity $\Omega_0$. When the temperature gradient is sufficient, instabilities develop within a thin layer near the equator of the inner cylinder (analogous to the Earth's equator), restricting convection to this band. These instabilities generate thermal waves that transport heat from the hot outer wall toward the cooler inner wall. In this work, we present rigorous upper and lower bounds valid in all regimes regarding the total heat flux—the sum of conductive and convective components—as a function of the rotation rate. In the specific case of pure conduction, these bounds establish the famous Rayleigh–Prandtl number variation with the Rossby number. Our approach leverages Fourier series expansions to decompose all nonlinear terms into their spectral contributions. The resulting bounds exhibit an approximate $1/\Omega_0^2$ dependence characterized by rotationally symmetric modes indexed by the Rossby number. We validate these bounds experimentally, demonstrating that the rotational enhancement of the Rayleigh–Prandtl number follows the predicted $1/\Omega_0^2$ scaling. Consequently, our findings provide both theoretical and experimental confirmation of the rotationally modified Rayleigh–Prandtl number $\hat{R}\equiv \frac {Rp^2}{\Omega _0^2}$ (or simply the $R^*\equiv \frac {R}{\Omega _0^2}$) as the appropriate parameter to evaluate rotational effects on the nonlinear heat transfer. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for directly measuring the Nusselt number in rotating annulus experiments. Utilizing this technique, we conducted experiments across a broad spectrum of rotation rates, revealing that the rotational enhancement of heat transfer adheres to the proposed bounds up to a critical threshold defined by the Rayleigh–Prandtl number. These results support a recently proposed model for the nonlinear heat transfer of the rotating annulus that relies on spectral decomposition. These findings have significant implications for understanding how rotation influences nonlinear heat transfer in various fluid systems. Finally, we show that the proposed model accounts for the observed $0.25$ power-law scaling of the Nusselt number with respect to the Rayleigh–Prandtl number in rotating annulus experiments. Although this approach allows for the use of threshold-invariant extreme value parameters, the interdependence among these parameters complicates estimation. We introduce a new estimation method that uncovers this underlying structure of dependence to improve estimation efficiency by considering the correlation between parameters. This proposal can be viewed as a form of covariate adjustment within threshold-exceedance modeling, where time serves as the implicit covariate. Our framework extends this concept of adjustment to account for additional explicit covariates. The proposed method is evaluated through simulations, with results showing that it performs comparably to maximum likelihood estimation when parameters are uncorrelated and significantly outperforms them when thresholds are sparse, given that parameters are correlated. The approach is also applied to two datasets, highlighting substantial improvements in estimation accuracy. A limitation is that, unlike standard likelihood-based methods, our procedure does not yield standard errors for the estimated parameters; a proposed future research direction addresses this by introducing a bootstrap approach to calculate standard errors without requiring a first-order asymptotic approximation. Additionally, the method supports the use of a single global threshold-invariant parameter, the tail index, enabling the fully parametric fitting of extreme value distributions. This capability enhances downstream applications of estimated distributions, such as calculating quantiles, return levels, or exceedance probabilities, and facilitates cross-validation between different datasets. Our findings demonstrate that this approach effectively removes bias arising from approximation errors in parametric extensions, resulting in more accurate estimates for extreme values, quantiles, and return levels when fitting extreme value distributions. The method is compatible with other parametric approaches for extreme value modeling, offering greater flexibility in modeling the frequency component of extreme value processes. This is particularly useful for correcting biases caused by simplifying assumptions regarding frequency patterns. The approach can be adapted for other parametric models for extreme value data with a fixed tail index that are estimated via threshold-exceedance data, provided frequency parameters are modeled as constants rather than time-varying. This includes cases where parameters are time-dependent but exhibit no trend, as well as scenarios where they depend on external covariates. The method remains applicable to other contexts in extreme value analysis, such as the generalized Pareto distribution or peak-over-threshold modeling. Finally, this approach represents just one application of the broader principle of dependent variable estimation, which addresses efficiency losses from ignoring correlations among threshold-exceedance parameters. In a setting where an adversary can arbitrarily alter an $\epsilon$ fraction of the state-action-reward-next-state tuples in a batch dataset, the learner's objective is to derive a near-optimal policy from the corrupted data. We first establish that for linear MDPs of dimension $d$, a worst-case optimality gap of $\Omega(d\epsilon)$ is inevitable, even when corruption is limited to the reward component alone. This finding differs from dimension-free bounds in robust supervised learning and contrasts with the best-known lower bounds for online RL under corruption. Subsequently, we introduce robust adaptations of the Least-Square Value Iteration (LSVI) algorithm, leveraging robust supervised learning oracles to achieve near-optimal performance whether full data coverage exists or not. In scenarios lacking coverage, the algorithm necessitates prior knowledge of $\epsilon$ to construct the policy, a requirement we later address in an adaptation that infers $\epsilon$ automatically. Our theoretical analysis provides near-optimal upper bounds and demonstrates improved robustness compared to prior research. Furthermore, we examine automata-based models of corruption to derive tightness results relative to standard adversarial settings. Experimental validation on continuous control environments confirms that our proposed algorithms outperform previous offline RL methods in both clean and corrupted datasets. Collectively, these efforts represent one of the initial attempts to address adversarial corruption in offline RL, and our results indicate that the resulting theoretical guarantees are tight. These findings suggest that robustifying offline RL against adversarial corruption is a challenging endeavor that demands a degree of prior assumptions regarding corruption structure. Ultimately, this research aims to complement studies on data augmentation by exploring adversarial perspectives.

We present a straightforward approach for automatically generating diverse datasets to train robust reinforcement learning policies that maintain performance on data distributed outside the original environment's support. Our method is simple, trainable independently of the main RL task, and applicable to various models and datasets, even when only a single environment is available. We evaluate this approach's efficacy in scenarios involving support shifts, a phenomenon uncommon in the training data but present in the test domain, a challenge that has remained largely unaddressed until now. Extensive evaluations across multiple simulated domains demonstrate that our proposed methods surpass prior work in handling support shifts, with results on larger, more complex datasets expected to provide insights for medical imaging applications. We have made the code and pre-trained models available at \url{https://github.com/bertinappa/diverse-datasets-robust-rl}.
