Results indicate that at most M-dwarf wavelengths, the spectra of white-light flares differ minimally from quiescent spectra. This implies that white light during stellar flares mostly originates from photospheric emission. Furthermore, our findings suggest that chromospheric reflection is unlikely to contribute to white light due to the low-temperature coronas typical of M-dwarfs. Finally, we investigate various scattering models to constrain the expected spectral characteristics. Our findings align well with recent theoretical developments within the "chromospheric mirror" framework. These results support the hypothesis that white-light M-dwarf flare emission results from electron heating of the lower atmosphere, which unobscures the photosphere to allow more visible starlight to escape. This provides a scattering explanation for white-light M-dwarf flares that advances our understanding of stellar flare physics. Given these findings, future detailed spectral analyses of M-dwarf flare events can further refine our models of chromospheric reflection. Moreover, obtaining M-dwarf flare spectra will be essential for validating simplified emission models currently used to explore planetary atmospheres. To address this, we introduce a two-stage training framework for point cloud generation that employs a sharpness constraint-optimized generator alongside a discriminator. In the initial stage, both the discriminator and generator are trained concurrently under a standard adversarial setup. We provide comprehensive insights into both cooperative and non-cooperative scenarios through theoretical analysis and simulations. Our findings indicate that, for the same parameters, both approaches achieve high spectral efficiency, though the cooperative method does so with significantly less complexity. Although a minor performance drop occurs at very short chirps-per-second rates, the difference between cooperative and non-cooperative spectral efficiency remains negligible for longer durations. Additionally, the proposed detection theory, which accounts for potential interference, is demonstrated to be 40 percent more sensitive than a standard orthogonal orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (O-OFDM) implementation. Finally, we outline the specific modifications required to enable radars to coordinate with one another.

Wired sensor networks are emerging as a promising data-collection technology for energy-sensitive applications, including structural and machine health monitoring. However, fusing data from multiple sensors to extend measurement duration and minimize power usage is complicated by two main issues: first, correlations between sensors reduce the information value of individual readings, and second, quantization errors can cause aliasing that mimics the correlation structures of other sensors. This study addresses these challenges and introduces a methodology to determine the optimal number of sensors and sampling rate for complete spectral recovery. Two distinct scenarios are analyzed: (1) when cross-correlations are known and (2) when they are unknown. We show that knowledge of cross-correlations allows the network to achieve the same sampling rate as independent sensors but with fewer sensors, or to reduce latency by using fewer sensors at a cost of higher sampling rates. Furthermore, we develop tests to estimate the maximum aliasing caused by ignoring cross-correlations and prove that combining these tests with the proposed methodology enables complete spectral recovery at the lowest possible sampling rate. Simulation results indicate that ignoring cross-correlations can lead to a 50 percent reduction in the achievable sampling rate. The proposed solution is implemented in Python, available as an open-source code.

This work examines the impact of incorporating channel state information (CSI) into channel-dependent OFDM-based wireless sensor network (WSN) protocols. It details how to extend existing channel-agnostic MAC protocols to leverage channel conditions and compares their performance against fully channel-agnostic baselines. Our findings indicate that channel-aware scheduling can substantially boost network throughput. Specifically

This work introduces a novel approach by analyzing the nonlinearity of the Intense Box-Car Autocorrelator (IBCA) signal, which serves as a time-resolved method for ETPA. To enable this signal generation, a femtosecond laser was used to simultaneously excite a mixture of Tolane (TOL) and DEVA (4-pentyn-1-ol-1,7-dinitro) within a 2-mm thick cuvette. Time resolution was achieved by manipulating the relative delays between the TOL and DEVA beams using a pair of dichroic mirrors. The presence of ETPA was confirmed by comparing the observed EICA signal with theoretical calculations that incorporate both single-photon (SPA) and two-photon (TPA) absorption components. Time-resolved EICA spectra were obtained without the need for upconversion detection. Furthermore, time-of-flight mass spectrometry (TOF-MS) was employed to investigate fragmentation channels, while the simultaneous measurement of EICA and TOF-MS data clarified variations in ETPA probabilities. Additionally, the effects of solvent type and concentration on ETPA were examined. Finally, a discussion is provided regarding the applicability of this technique for time-resolving ETPA processes. In summary, the results demonstrate that this method is effective for time-resolving ETPA in liquid solutions.

This paper investigates an idealized ground-sound model grounded in elastodynamic halfspace theory to determine when such sound is perceptually significant versus when it is obscured by the object's modal tones or transient acceleration noise. Our analytical approach yields a smooth, closed-form formula for ground surface acceleration, which can be applied via the Rayleigh integral or as an "acoustic shader" within finite-difference time-domain wave simulations. We conclude that when modal sounds are inaudible, ground sound becomes audible only for dense objects striking rigid surfaces; in this scenario, impact duration scales proportionally with the object's radius. This result validates our earlier hypothesis that for hard objects like bullets or hail, ground sound is typically audible, whereas for soft objects such as apples, it is always masked. Our simulation models enable efficient rendering of ground sound for visual feedback during impact sound design. Finally, this study offers a smooth extension to halfspace theory that remains accurate through contact separation, a refinement essential for synthesizing the brief "click" phase of a complete impact event.

Our custom audio capture system records field sounds for use in real-time interactive sound design software. During sound exploration, recorded samples appear as playback parameters; when selected, they display a feature-based summary to assist creators in navigating their samples. This method, known as authoring by remembrance, supports creativity by encouraging experimentation beyond familiar tools and techniques. In this paper, we present over a dozen captured ground sounds from various environments, demonstrate how audio parameters influence their visual representations, and discuss the creative advantages of authoring by remembrance. We hope this work inspires further research into hybrid audio-visual pipelines for assisted sound creation.

Synthesizing impact sounds presents a difficult challenge for game audio designers due to the vast variability in real-world materials. While existing research offers solutions for visually consistent objects on visually consistent surfaces, current methods fail to address combinations involving visually inconsistent materials. Visually inconsistent materials include objects or surfaces with varying sizes, drop heights, hardness levels, and compositions. Visually based synthesis relies on converting surface geometry into high-frequency mesh spectra, producing realistic sounds by leveraging the coupling between surface vibration and airborne acoustic radiation. However, this conversion is computationally intensive and impractical for interactive applications. To address this, we introduce a new material classification scheme where visually consistent objects hitting visually consistent surfaces are labeled CC, visually inconsistent objects on visually consistent surfaces as CI, and visually consistent objects on visually inconsistent surfaces as IC. Visually inconsistent surfaces are denoted as VC and WC. Visually based synthesis

This study explores the nonlocal consequences of local hidden-variable models satisfying specific conditions to establish an inequality that contradicts quantum mechanics in a similar manner. We derive this inequality for general qubit systems and demonstrate that violations occur not only due to experimental errors but also when relaxing certain detection efficiency requirements within local hidden-variable models. Furthermore, we provide numerical evidence showing that these detections-efficient all-versus-nothing proofs remain completely noise-free. Additionally, these efficiency-based all-versus-nothing proofs offer a more straightforward method for verifying detection efficiency, thereby serving as a complementary approach to existing techniques. Finally, these proofs can be extended to other forms of Bell nonlocality, such as those relying on Bell inequalities like CHSH or those without witnesses. Last, but not least, these detection efficiency-based all-versus-nothing proofs represent a unique type of proof that is entirely free from contextuality assumptions. Our findings indicate that all-versus-nothing proofs providing complete noise-free guarantees for local hidden-variable models are exceptionally rare. By utilizing a molecular orbital (MO) framework for flat band systems, random MO models are developed that maintain degeneracy in the non-randomized limit. Applying a perturbation approach to these models, exact second-order results are determined. Flat band systems are characterized by Riesz conditions and exceptional sets; consequently, density of states (DOS) formulas are established for both two- and three-dimensional cases. It is established that in dimension $d\geq 2$, the DOS is concentrated near an interval $B$ with a magnitude proportional to $l^{d-1}$, where $l$ represents the mean free path. Specifically, the DOS is estimated as $\delta(\{0\}) = c_0 \frac{1}{(l_0)^{d+1}}$ and $\delta(\{1\}) = c_1 \frac{1}{(l_1)^{d+1}}$, with $l_0$ and $l_1$ representing the mean free paths for states at the Fermi energy when it is set to $-1$ and $1$, respectively. Furthermore, the $\delta(\mathcal{E})$-measure is demonstrated to be non-zero within a range proportional to $l^{-1}$. Exact DOS expressions are provided for the square lattice, simple cubic lattice, and $(n+1)$-simplex lattice. The validity of the DOS estimates is confirmed by their alignment with the delocalized regime of the $npd$-model's spectrum. Additionally, the flat band model exhibits an insulating ground state under certain conditions.

This work presents a generalization of the Fibonacci-Stirling numbers, which can map the set of integers $\{1,2, \ldots ,n\}$ to the set $\{0,1, \ldots ,n-1\}$ in $F_{n+1}$ ways, where $F_n$ denotes the $n$-th Fibonacci number. Our investigation relies on characterizing the linear boundedness of almost simple algebraic groups with a parabolic subgroup defined over $K$. This identification involves examining the geometric complexity of semisimple varieties, specifically by demonstrating that the tangent bundle of a semisimple variety remains nonnegatively bounded, is trivial in the affine case, and that the tangent bundle of a reductive group always possesses trivial vector bundles as direct summands. Furthermore, our work elucidates the algebraic, topological, and analytic structures of linear bounded groups, revealing a fundamental connection between their algebraic and topological properties. Additionally, we examine smoothness in the analytic topology for groups of Lie type over local fields, as well as in the analytic and algebraic topologies for tori. These constructions highlight a deeper relationship between the algebraic, topological, and analytic nature of a group and its vectorized tangent bundle. Finally, we note that all varieties under consideration are smooth, irreducible, and complete over $K$. These arithmetic groups exhibit geometric complexity and include both semisimple and reductive types. Our results suggest a new strategy for investigating the arithmetic of tangent bundles and the algebraic, topological, and analytic structures of linear bounded groups through the lens of analytic geometry and homotopy theory. This approach represents a novel methodology in number theory, offering a distinct framework that differs from current approaches in the field. Additionally, the geometric complexity of semisimple varieties serves as a key criterion for classifying varieties by their topological and algebraic structures. This geometric complexity may also characterize the homotopy type of the tangent bundle for reductive groups, encompassing both negative and positive cases. The homotopy type in the negative case corresponds to a projective space with a shift in dimension equal to the rank of the group, while the positive case remains an open problem that could represent a significant advancement in arithmetic geometry. Moreover, the arithmetic of nonnegatively bounded tangent bundles may characterize the arithmetic of tangent bundles in reductive groups via a topological criterion. The topological criterion encompasses aspects of a group's algebraic structure, topological dimension, and the dimensions of its homogeneous spaces. The algebraic and topological criteria may characterize the local invariants of a group, including both topological and Galois covariant variants. Our approach represents a novel architecture in arithmetic geometry

Achieving this necessitates redundant architectures and a mechanism to reconfigure the system upon failure, typically implemented through arbitration logic. To ensure functional safety, the transition to a fail-operational state must be detectable, verifiable, and recognizable (DV0). The arbitration logic must incorporate this capability to meet safety standards. This paper presents a formal, model-based design approach for a high-integrity fail-operational driver system and explores the impact of the DV0 requirement on arbitration logic within drivers. We detail the arbitration layer and its integration into the driver, and we examine how formal methods were utilized to verify both functional correctness and safety obligations. A key finding is that formulating and verifying arbitration functions and fail-operational states for a complete driver system is significantly more complex than previously assumed, with the DV0 obligation adding substantial difficulty to the design and verification process. Additionally, a detailed comparison is drawn between fail-safe and fail-operational systems. The present work is based on a PhD thesis [1].

By identifying patterns of interaction within complex systems, this task separates active nodes into groups based on their degree of connectivity. These groups often correspond to distinct communities or social circles. This study focuses on detecting communities within engineering and social systems using a graph-based approach, where nodes—such as people or machines—are connected by edges that reflect various criteria. We developed a novel algorithm that fuses the advantages of the Advancing, Replacing, and Restoring (ARR) method with a new feature called Systematic Rounding (SR). The SR component minimizes the computational cost of the merging phase in ARR, which can range from quadratic to cubic relative to the number of nodes, by reducing it to linear complexity. Furthermore, our proposed algorithm demonstrates the ability to achieve lower within-community diameter values compared to the standard ARR approach. We validated these findings through experiments on standard real-world systems, confirming that the new SR-enhanced variant of ARR successfully identifies communities that standard ARR cannot. Additionally, we established a new benchmark for low within-community diameter using a Modified Random Graph model. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithm meets this benchmark, producing more uniform community distributions in terms of node degree than existing state-of-the-art community detection algorithms. Additionally, the algorithm is more than 10,000, 20,000, and 65,000 times faster than the Advancing and Restoring (AR), Advancing and Replacing and Restoring (R), and full ARR algorithms, respectively. This work introduces a new, highly efficient method for systematic node degree distribution, thereby advancing the current state-of-the-art in community detection. Finally, we provide a thorough analysis of how the proposed ARSR algorithm performs under different network conditions.

Based on tomographic redshift slices, we formulate a machine learning approach to estimate multiplicative redshift evolution biases when utilizing redshift-space data for cosmological parameter constraints. Additionally, we design several survey fiducial schemes to determine the data's constraining power on these parameters. We employ two distinct sets of bias parameters to represent evolution effects: (i) primarity (10 slices) and (ii) realism (5 slices), both within the redshift range $0.3<z<2.0$. Our findings indicate that the intensity of HI emission allows the spectra to probe biases, resulting in $10.8$ and $5.4\%$ uncertainties on $H_0$ and $\Omega_b$, respectively, under ideal conditions. When both HI intensity and temperature are accessed, uncertainties improve to $7.8\%$ and $3.2\%$ for $H_0$ and $\Omega_b$, achieving a $28\%$ and $41\%$ improvement over DESI constraints. We also quantify systematic errors, including those from EFTofLSS, tomographic binning, beam smoothing, foreground contamination, and baryonic feedback, all of which significantly degrade the constraints on cosmological parameters. Ultimately, these results demonstrate the immense potential of intensity mapping for measuring cosmological parameters. However, to achieve tighter constraints, future studies must address the mentioned systematic uncertainties, thereby unlocking the full power of large-scale HI observations for cosmology. Hasannasab noted that for a sequence of vectors $(e_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, the existence of an operator $T$ mapping $e_n$ to $e_{n+1}$ implies that the sequence is linearly independent if and only if the dimension of the span of these vectors is infinite. This article re-establishes that finding as a specific instance of a broader model-theoretic result grounded in order theory. Subsequently, we examine vector spaces to demonstrate that replacing the condition $T(e_n) = e_{n+1}$ with a more general "next element" relation preserves the core outcome, even when the sequence $(e_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is arbitrary. We conclude by applying this generalized result to the special linear group $\hbox{SL}_2(\mathbb{K})$. Furthermore, as an illustration of the power of model theory, we successfully solve a problem that was previously considered nearly impossible to address using traditional methods. This issue was initially raised in October 2020 on MathOverflow.

The 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a recent innovation for image recognition, has proven successful in capturing local similarities within 2D data. solving the Einstein equations requires addressing a system of coupled, nonlinear partial differential equations. This process includes a constraint equation that must be satisfied both initially and throughout the evolution. The "moving puncture" technique is currently the standard method for handling singularities arising from mass distributions. However, when the matter source includes a horizon, this method fails to properly enforce the constraint across the horizon surface. This paper presents a technique for implementing the constraint equation on such horizons using Kerr-Schild coordinates. We validate this approach through numerical tests, specifically checking the constraint equation around black hole Apparent Horizons using the Schwarzschild metric combined with a step-function matter distribution. Although this study uses the simple Step-function Matter Distribution (SMD) for demonstration, the method is applicable to more intricate cases, including cases without horizons, in various numerical relativity simulations. Finally, we discuss the broader applications of this approach within the context of the Einstein-Schrödinger equation. In conclusion, this work serves as foundational research for future studies. This approach is also relevant for other forces within the Standard Model that feature a Higgs field possessing a potential minimum. In this paper, we refer to this minimum as a "hollow."

To improve prediction accuracy, research has focused on enhancing pre-trained models through fine-tuning on downstream tasks, often by stacking multiple pre-trained languages on top of existing ones. However, fine-tuning individual language models is resource-intensive, making the training and integration of new models in ensemble ensemble a significant challenge. We introduce LaMaCollect, a novel ensemble technique that addresses this issue by training an "ensemble selector"—a lightweight multi-headed attention network—to select among pre-trained language models within an ensemble. Our results demonstrate that LaMaCollect outperforms both the individual models in the ensemble and several strong baseline selectors, such as Auto-Ensemble and Attention Over Time, when evaluated on eight English and three low-resource downstream tasks. Additionally, our ensemble selector can adapt to new models at no cost, a flexibility that is crucial for maintaining the ensemble's accuracy as new pre-trained models become available. Blurred image restoration is a persistent challenge in both theory and practice, finding applications in diverse fields such as digital photography, satellite imaging, and medical imaging, all of which demand efficient algorithms. Over the past decades, significant research has defined the problem mathematically and explored its solution space. A common modeling approach formulates restoration as a minimization problem with a data fidelity term: \[ \min_{u\in L^2(\Omega)}\int_{\Omega} |\delta (u(x)) - v(x)|^2\mbox{d}x, \] where $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is a bounded open square representing the image domain, $v(x)$ is the blurred image, and $\delta$ is a linear operator. , locating habitats, hunting, evading predators, and finding mates. The vast diversity of life has resulted in a wide array of locomotive strategies, from swimming in the ocean to climbing trees. A primary objective in locomotion research is to discover new, efficient movement methods for a specific environment. This study investigates whether such methods can be derived through an evolutionary process. Swapping between different locomotion strategies incurs metabolic costs; for instance, a fish leaving water must climb, or a mammal hunting on the ground must first locate prey. These costs create a trade-off, favoring a unified locomotion strategy that minimizes the sum of traveling and searching expenses. We propose using this combined cost as a fitness function to evolve new strategies. The search space comprises all possible strategies, defined as sequences of motor commands that generate specific cost landscapes. To investigate whether this space contains multiple strategies that perform comparably well, we apply a genetic algorithm to discover a diverse set of strategies. Results indicate that several strategies emerge that allow animals to reach the target directly from the habitat without an initial search. However, this comes at a price: these strategies are more sensitive to uncertainty regarding the target's location. Furthermore, different strategies exhibit varying tolerances to noise in motor commands. This research underscores a critical challenge in designing or discovering new locomotion methods: while such innovation may reduce individual metabolic cost during task execution, it can increase vulnerability to disturbances or threats. Additionally, multiple strategies exist that yield similar total costs, implying that environmental factors or random mutations could drive the selection of one over another. This paper demonstrates that a single metric for fitness can inadvertently promote unitarization in multi-agent systems. Finally, we highlight a limitation in applying unitarization concepts to autonomous driving, noting that new strategies may demand greater cognitive effort to execute, suggesting that fitness should be multi-dimensional to prevent the discovery of potentially hazardous strategies.

However, existing data-driven approaches typically neglect a critical aspect: the intrinsic physics, particularly conservation laws, should inherently constrain the learning process. This study introduces a new family of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) called "conservation-aware neural networks" (CANNs), which integrate conservation law constraints directly into the neural network architecture rather than adding them as post-processing terms to the loss function. This architecture specifically ensures that the regression problem remains well-posed and optimizes both the network parameters and regression weight simultaneously. Finally, we illustrate the method's versatility by applying it to determine the time-periodic Navier-Stokes equations. Our findings indicate that CANNs offer significant advantages over standard PINNs in inverse problems, potentially offering similar benefits for related physics-informed machine learning tasks. Furthermore, this approach can be readily extended to a broad spectrum of PDEs and data-fitting scenarios, suggesting its utility in solving important imaging problems. Indeed, we are exploring this possibility in collaboration with image scientists.

strict preference lists, requiring that no two agents mutually prefer each other over their current partners. While a linear-time solution exists for even-sized agent sets with mutual preferences, the problem becomes significantly more complex when odd-sized agents must remain unmatched. This paper introduces a cubic-time solution for general agent sets with mutual preferences, successfully identifying two agents without a stable partnership. This approach is achieved by adapting the quadratic cubic-time algorithm by Ashkenasi, Frisch, and Plumeau, which was originally created for the even-set case. The method involves constructing an orientable three-dimensional mesh of tripartite graphs and pairing agents by locating Hamiltonian paths within specific slices of this mesh. We demonstrate that for the case where all agent sets are odd, the overall complexity reduces to $O(n^{2.38})$, where $n$ represents the number of agents. This optimization is possible by omitting certain slices in the mesh construction, leveraging the fact that every 3-regular planar graph is outerplanar. Furthermore, we present a linear-time solution for specific instances where only two agents share the same preference list. However, we also demonstrate that no faster than cubic-time algorithm exists when agents have varying preference lists, as reducing the input to the minimum possible size does not improve the lower bound derived from a known cubic-time construction. This result contrasts with the minimum-time solution existence for the even-set case, established by Plumeau. Finally, we examine how to resolve the problem by allowing a constant number of agents to remain unmatched, a variant that holds practical relevance. In this scenario, a linear-time solution exists for the even set of agents, while a cubic-time solution is required for the general set. This is accomplished by building an orientable three-dimensional mesh of tripartite graphs and finding a perfect matching in each tripartite graph to match most agents, followed by resolving the few remaining agents.

Subsequent analysis reveals that all clouds fall into two categories: the trivial cloud over the Hilbert space containing the complete Gromov--Hausdorff universe, and clouds derived via cloud deflation, which are fundamentally linked to metric Banach spaces. This classification is deeply connected to cloud completeness and the cloud completeness problem first posed by Gromov. By integrating cloud theory with the metric completion process, we demonstrate that every compact space universe is completeness dense in a completeness space universe, with the exception of the Banach space derived from the compact convex subsets of $L_{\infty}$. Final work addresses an old problem by Rigby, which asks whether the Gromov--Hausdorff distance can distinguish non-isomorphic complete separable metric spaces. Our findings indicate that the answer is negatively linked to the existence of a universal completeness space cloud that is also a metric space cloud. Consequently, developing rapid and adaptable decoding algorithms capable of handling faulty syndrome measurements is essential. This study demonstrates that decoding these codes within a full fault-tolerant framework can be naturally recast as repeated interactions between a decoder and its environment, enabling the application of reinforcement learning to train decoding agents. As a proof of concept, we utilized deep Q-learning to create fast decoding agents for the surface code across various noise models. Additionally, we introduced a hierarchical training approach that decouples the agent from specific noise characteristics and syndrome structure; this method yields faster convergence and produces agents capable of accurately decoding faulty frames. We further show that these trained agents generalize effectively to topological codes beyond the surface code, including the triangular and honeycomb codes, and the color, LDPC, and Ravichandran-Veeraraghavan codes. Furthermore, we establish that decoding agents can be engineered to achieve fault tolerance below the theoretical code threshold while simultaneously maintaining acceptable logical error rates. Finally, we propose a technique for creating a hierarchical agent architecture that facilitates the adaptation of a universal decoding agent to unknown noise models with exceptional precision. By engaging with the environment during logical computation, these agents continuously improve their performance, demonstrating the potential for adaptive error correction. We anticipate that this work will inspire extensive research into advanced decoding strategies for fault-tolerant quantum computers. As a starting point, we have made our code definitions, decoding agents, and training scripts accessible for further investigation.

In interferometry, this is usually accomplished by evolving an initial high-entropy state along a highly curved path, ultimately yielding a low-entropy final state where correlations peak to achieve maximum precision. This work introduces a novel quantum metrology scheme centered not on generating correlations, but on minimizing the support of the quantum state. Precision is enhanced by moving the quantum support away from the boundary of the Hamiltonian's zero-energy sector, termed the minimal support set. This approach maintains the quantum support within this invariant set throughout the evolution. As the support expands away from the set, the state rapidly converges to a small collection of nearly pure quasi-orthogonal vectors. This creates a highly entangled, few-mode basis where the support reaches its maximum at the end of evolution, marking the optimal measurement point. This quantum metrology occurs naturally without requiring fine-tuned control of the quantum support or the search for an unknown optimal state. Furthermore, the method enables metrology in scenarios where correlations alone cannot be effectively harnessed for precision gains. This includes cases involving large decoherence during evolution and situations where the available Hamiltonian lacks the necessary modes to create the required correlations. The latter case represents a new resource for metrology; we illustrate this with a proof-of-concept example using the Rydberg atom array Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we show that this mechanism can be utilized to precisely measure thermal parameters. The proposed quantum metrology is generally applicable to any open quantum system with a quantum control Hamiltonian. Notably, it does not demand more qubits than the device under investigation and may offer a path to more practical quantum metrology schemes.

Recently, numerous quantum many-body systems have been engineered in laboratory settings to exhibit long-living topological orders. We establish the existence of a novel class of long-living topological phases within quantum many-body systems driven by a time-periodic Hamiltonian, known as topological stable limit sets (TSLs). TSLs represent a new type of long-living topological order in quantum many-body limit sets. We present a general framework for defining TSLs and their topological order, demonstrating their presence in a periodic quantum spin chain. In this system, the quantum many-body limit set is established by a family of time-periodic product states. We prove that these long-living topological phases are fragile, meaning even minor additional perturbations to the driving protocol can cause their complete destruction.

We demonstrate the application of this digital-hybrid approach to spin systems featuring always-on Ising interactions. By utilizing finite-duration microwave pulses that simultaneously couple qubits and drive Rabi oscillations, we implement quantum operations that progress in sync with evolution under always-on interactions. We show that a specific collection of these microwave-pulse-modified basis changes and unitary rotations forms a universal gate set for digital-hybrid quantum computing. We illustrate the algorithm's capabilities through a case study involving Bell inequality optimization, where experiments on superconducting qubit platforms serve to validate the method's experimental feasibility. Furthermore, we examine the performance of the method across various platforms, including transmon qubits and trapped ions, highlighting its adaptability to different qubit technologies. Finally, we assess the algorithm's resilience against experimental noise and computational errors, as well as its capacity to process Arbitrary Waveform Generator (AWG) quantization errors. These findings underscore the potential of the digital-hybrid model to streamline near-term quantum experiments and accelerate progress toward large-scale quantum technologies.\par

Multimodal learning has garnered significant attention within the context of quantum machine learning (QML). Existing research indicates that employing multiple input types can boost classification performance, yet current approaches often depend on noisy readouts or a limited number of output classes, constraining their applicability to complex, high-dimensional data. This study introduces a novel multimodal learning strategy that utilizes shared entangled measurements to process diverse input modality pairs. This technique not only enhances readout accuracy and classification success rates but also functions effectively with arbitrary output dimensions, maintaining robustness even under high readout noise conditions. We validate these findings using 2019 Nobel Prize-winning quantum entanglement data, supplemented by additional experiments involving optical imaging data. Our results demonstrate that this digital-hybrid multimodal approach is readily adaptable to current superconducting qubit architectures and other emerging quantum technology platforms.\par

We propose a universal gate set composed of modified basis changes and microwaves that run in conjunction with always-on interactions. In direct imaging surveys, the probability of detecting a planet is strongly tied to its weather regime and orbital distance. To better predict these detection probabilities, we created a novel planet population synthesis model that integrates state-of-of-the-art planet formation theory with next-generation instrument capabilities. This model simulates planetary formation and evolution from the protoplanetary disk through the planetary system, incorporating key physical properties like mass and orbital distance. We projected a virtual planet population formed under this framework onto the Next Generation Exoplanet Imaging instrument (NGTIES) detection parameter space by simulating ten-year survey data. Our results indicate that this synthesis approach predicts several potentially detectable Jupiter-mass planets with semi-major axes exceeding 2 AU within such surveys. Furthermore, we developed an advanced deep learning image simulation tool integrated with the synthesis code to artificially generate survey data, which was then analyzed using real observational data. Our findings reveal that NGTIES will achieve approximately 69% completeness in detecting Jupiter-mass planets with semi-major axes greater than 2.5 AU among those with a dynamical contrast lower than 70% of the Hill sphere pressure, a figure that remains relatively stable despite uncertainties in planet formation and evolution models. Consequently, the anticipated discovery rate of such planets from a single star could range from zero to three over a ten-year period, depending on stellar population variations. When combined, these predictions suggest that NGTIES may identify multiple such planets across different stellar populations within the coming decade. Therefore, robust planning and the utilization of pre-existing multi-epoch observational data will be essential to maximize the scientific return of these next-generation high-contrast imaging missions. This study provides a roadmap for anticipated planet population discoveries, offering a benchmark for future research. As a supplementary note, we detail our innovative methods for synthesis and image simulation, along with a public code release, to assist other researchers in artificially generating both new and simulated survey data. This study evaluates the potential of the upcoming DUNE experiment to detect sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Since the design of the Near Detector remains undetermined, we calculate the anticipated number of sterile neutrino decays within that volume. Our most optimistic projections suggest that the resulting constraints on mixing could be several orders of magnitude tighter than those found in previous studies. Additionally, we present design-dependent estimates for the "long" and particularly the very light sterile neutrino regimes. We conclude that, similar to recent findings for MiniBooNE, non-standard physics within nuclear fast-burst environments may generate signals as large as those produced by neutrino oscillations. Finally, we discuss how various selection criteria—both dependent and independent of the neutrino mass—can suppress these excessive backgrounds. Overall, our results indicate that DUNE is capable of exploring a vast region of the parameter space, potentially discovering the sterile neutrino. These conclusions can be extended to other nuclear accelerator-based experiments undergoing upgrades to large detector systems. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed constraints requires detailed simulations of the neutrino flux, including detailed modeling of the neutrator response. We also address how to test for evidence of the sterile neutrino when the sensitivity is not sufficient to measure the mixing angle directly. In this scenario, we propose to characterize the residual dependence on the neutrino mass by comparing the shape of the energy spectrum in fast-burst experiments. We address the potential for misidentifying fast-burst effects as oscillation signals and show that statistical tests can distinguish between the two. We conclude by comparing our proposed sensitivity of DUNE with the current state-of-the-art. We note that, like previous fast-burst experiments, the signal may be too weak to discover the sterile neutrino, even when projections for the number of oscillation dips and peaks are significant. However, with fast-burst experiments, the signal is expected to be oscillation-like only when sterile neutrinos are produced in nuclei. In this case, the background can be controlled to reduce uncertainties to a level where the sterile neutrino is discoverable. This strategy is also applicable to other fast-burst experiments, although with reduced sensitivity. We demonstrate that the probability of the sterile neutrino's existence across its parameter space can be constrained to less than one percent before the start of the DUNE data-taking period. While cluster-robust variance-covariance estimators offer a viable method for synthesizing these dependent effects, current state-of-the-art techniques may produce inflated Type 1 errors when the number of studies is limited. To address this, we introduce two novel cluster-robust estimators designed to enhance performance in small samples. This work examines the dynamics of a liquid jet issuing from a channel into a free surface of the same liquid, serving as a fundamental model for phenomena such as peninsular dissolution, venturi instability, and air entrainment. While a analytical theory exists for the idealized scenario of pure penetration—where a thin jet of incompressible, Newtonian fluid enters a channel of a matching fluid without accounting for the sheath and collapse cycles characteristic of viscous jets—our analytical, numerical, and experimental analyses reveal a more complex reality. Specifically, we observe a initial growth of an air sheath around the jet followed by a collapse cycle that occurs before the peninsular reaches the channel ends. Our comprehensive theoretical framework extends the previous limited theory to incorporate these full penetration and collapse cycles. These techniques are designed to determine distribution functions for physically realizable configurations at a fixed energy and angular momentum, creating a challenge where variables are redundant and physically constrained. Although standard theories typically ascribe both forms to galactic tidal interactions with massive companions, T-arches have been predominantly observed in late-type systems, leading some researchers to propose that gravitational interaction is solely responsible for creating T-arches. Specifically, photons interact with quasiparticles whose electronic components are already responding; thus, attributing the response to the "naked" electrons would be misleading. Furthermore, my analysis reveals that effective responses can be either amplified or redirected. For instance, the magnetic response of a TI is not merely a minor correction to electric conduction, as in ordinary materials, but is instead so significantly strengthened by the bulk that it dominates the total response. These findings suggest that effective responses in TIs can be primarily driven by components that would be negligible in standard insulators. Finally, I contend that these findings offer valuable insights into responding to quasiparticles during chemical reactions. Typically, responses are thought to occur between naked particles because the energy cost of interactions is minimal compared to the response itself. However, in TIs, effective responses between quasiparticles are so strongly coupled that they exceed weak responses in ordinary insulators by several orders of magnitude. Therefore, TIs provide a unique platform for studying strongly coupled quasiparticle interactions. These newly discovered principles of response can substantially advance our understanding of various tissues. Specifically, my work offers hope for theoretically investigating strongly correlated electrons, strongly correlated photons, and other strongly correlated tissues. However, determining which specific issues are solved through design requires careful reasoning, and no prior approach exists to filter out non-design-related discussions. This study examines how designers and non-designers address issues within the design context across five collaborative coding projects. We introduce DesignDisc, a design issue classification method using 11 features, and DesignXpath, an automated method relying on three features. Our empirical findings indicate that Non-Design 1 issues are resolvable through design with 75% accuracy, whereas Non-Design 2 and Non-Design 3 are rarely or never doable, respectively. Both DesignDisc and DesignXpath demonstrate strong cross-project generalization capabilities. Additionally, designers and non-designers often perceive the doability of an issue differently, creating confusion and wasted effort. Finally, developers can largely infer the specific commits addressing doable non-design issues based on their roles. This approach leverages the pulse's time-of-flight (TOF) and bandwidth to achieve a resolution power significantly greater than the system's intrinsic resolution capability. By employing multiple detection events and applying Bayesian algorithms, we successfully detect and count rare quantum occurrences with high accuracy through repeated measurements. We have validated this method experimentally and extended it explicitly for quantum sensing applications, such as measuring optical transmission, quantum state tomography, and detecting dark matter axions. Additionally, we develop corresponding quantum and stochastic models to analyze various sensing and detection scenarios, addressing both single-shot and multiple-shot conditions. These frameworks address the correlation between measurement data and unknown parameters, as well as the impact of finite measurement counts on estimator accuracy. Key properties such as the quantum Cramér-Ramo bound (QCRB), classical Cramér-Ramo bound (CRB), mean-squared error (MSE), sampling efficiency, and finite-size estimator performance are explicitly calculated and assessed for physical relevance. The quantum estimator achieves a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement of approximately $10^4$ and maintains a high SNR of roughly $10^2$ compared to conventional optical detection systems. We anticipate that this device will serve as a valuable tool for quantum optics experiments and find applications in fields including quantum computing, communication, and metrology. Additionally, this method functions as a robust time-resolved detector capable of identifying rare quantum events—such as single photons and entangled particles—with sub-ns precision. However, data sensitivity and privacy concerns often hinder partnerships between municipalities and public-sector technology providers, creating a need for on-premise solutions. While many algorithms have emerged to tackle this problem, a prominent example is the CMA-ES evolution strategy, an unsupervised learning technique capable of navigating unstructured reward landscapes. Recent observations indicate that young stellar objects with strong magnetic field connections to their surrounding environment follow a log-normal distribution. This study examines if this distribution also applies to young stars lacking such environmental magnetic connections. Utilizing the 3D stochastic model \textit{twitch}, we analyze magnetic connections for a sample of 1,190 young stars with known masses and distances. For young stars not linked to their environment via a magnetic connection, our \textit{twitch} model successfully reproduces the observed characteristic value and slope of the log-normal distribution. This suggests that the logarithmic slope and characteristic value may be determined by two distinct magnetic connection mechanisms: one connecting the star to its environment, and the other failing to form a connection with the surrounding environment. Furthermore, our \textit{twitch} model characterizes this failing magnetic connection as a connection between the star and its circumstellar disc. This interpretation is supported by the fact that young stars with known distances also exhibit a log-normal distribution when considering only those lacking environmental magnetic connections. These consistent results across distance-based observations imply that a magnetic connection failing to form with the environment, while a connection with the disc is established, is a necessary condition for a young star to follow a log-normal distribution. Additionally, we explore the possibility that the turn-over observed at higher masses in observations and simple models like \textit{twitch} without stochastic angular momentum transport represents an observational limit rather than a physical constraint. Our findings suggest that young stars with strong disc connections, regardless of whether they have environmental magnetic connections, are more likely to evolve into higher-mass stars. This could help explain recent observations of higher-mass young stars exhibiting scattered values for X-ray luminosity and environmental magnetic connections. Finally, the stochastic nature of our \textit{twitch} model, particularly when combined with differential rotation in discs, may be a necessary condition for young stars with strong disc connections to follow a log-normal distribution, regardless of their environmental magnetic connections. This could offer an explanation for recent observations and complex numerical simulations showing that the distribution of young stars with strong disc connections adheres to a log-normal distribution. This paper examines association rules within finite Gaussian graphical models, which are undirected graphs where connected nodes signify independent subsets. In this context, each node corresponds to a binary random variable, and every implication within the association rule decomposition can be interpreted as independent set independence. We identify specific maximal independent sets whose interactions produce the dependent edges observed in the graphs of interest, thereby framing the problem of decomposing Gaussian graphical models into independent components as a dependency learning issue. We demonstrate that current literature establishes a connection between the difficulty of learning association rules and the presence of bounded degree or bounded clique size. However, we argue that this problem is significantly more tractable for Gaussian graphical models, as it suffices to learn across independent sets of bounded size even when the overall model exhibits unbounded clique size. This limitation arises because the independent sets identifying the model's causal structure possess a bounded size. We provide explicit bounds for both parameters. While existing theoretical frameworks exist, our main contribution is unifying these into a single, learnable framework for Gaussian graphical models. Subsequently, we develop a conceptually distinct formulation that maintains both bounded degree and bounded clique size. Although both parameters are independent of the bit complexity of the observed data, the primary distinction lies in the loss of clique size, although we offer strategies to mitigate this. Finally, we conduct an empirical comparison between our proposed formulation and the standard approach using public datasets. Although learning the max independent set size with guaranteed bounds is a more conservative assumption, experimental results indicate only a minor increase in empirical running time—less than a factor of two—compared to the standard formulation, despite ensuring bounded clique size. Furthermore, the suggested formulation exhibits superior scalability in terms of both bit complexity and the number of variables. While bonus appendix material details specific mathematical distinctness, our primary focus remains on empirically validating the feasibility and efficacy of learning bounded clique size. Ultimately, we conclude that the proposed formulation not only guarantees boundedness but also delivers higher accuracy than the existing state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we discuss the applicability of these results to feature selection and multi-omics data integration.

. This study evaluates a straightforward, cost-effective approach by concatenating original data instances to form augmented ones, termed "concat-augmentation." The method is simple and computationally inexpensive because it relies solely on the original data without needing additional indices. We explore enhancing this basic technique by concatenating instances from randomly selected batches rather than the entire dataset, thereby reducing computational costs. Furthermore, we develop a novel scheme to pre-process these concatenated sequences, enabling the model to distinguish between original data instances within a batch. Experiments on the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art augmentation techniques, such as Cutout and Random Erasing, while requiring less computation. Additionally, concat-augmentation yields more stable training, exhibits greater robustness, and serves as a viable alternative to complex augmentation strategies. We have made our implementation public at https://github.com/MohammadHosseinB/Concat-Augmentation. At present, concat-augmentation achieves SOTA performance on CIFAR10/100, requires lower computation than AUGMix and DTAug, trains more stably than Cutout and Random Erasing, and offers greater flexibility compared to ImageNet methods. A comprehensive analysis of these advantages is provided on CIFAR10/100. The approach is applicable to various architectures, including ResNet, MobileNetV2, VGG16, and more. Our results indicate an average accuracy improvement of +2.23% across all methods and architectures on both datasets. Finally, we emphasize that concat-augmentation is exceptionally efficient, trailing DTAug by 17% and AUGMix by 32% in computational cost on CIFAR10.

\paragraph{Related Work} The \textit{FedBuff} objective function represents a relaxed optimality criterion designed to ensure convergence even when gradients are both stale and noisy. This article also addresses questions posed by Bates and Sims, establishing that a specific category of countable parallel graphs, which do not require sources, are associated with simple C*-algebras. Our analysis of outside and inside moves, which represent partial answers to Bates and Sims, also confirms Sharp and Valette's discovery that the $C^*$-algebras of the "dual" Coxeter groups examined by Moody are either isomorphic or trivial. Our investigation is guided by the inquiry: under what conditions do parallel graphs yield simple $C^*$-algebras? We establish that countable parallel graphs featuring a single color possess simple $C^*$-algebras if and only if they lack a source and exhibit no periodic behavior confined to a single vertex orbit. While retrieving relevant snippets from these encyclopedias improves performance, it often results in a disjointed context that lacks cohesiveness. This study demonstrates that such a disconnected state prevents the unified processing of both the question and the retrieved context. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a two-stage addressable retrieval framework. In the first stage, the question is fed into the pre-trained LM to obtain a partial context. * We propose a two-stage addressable retrieval framework that shows multi-fold improvements over previous retrieval-based baselines.
* We introduce an multi-task learning approach to utilize external encyclopedias more effectively.
* We provide detailed analysis and ablation studies to evaluate the model's performance more comprehensively.
* We release a collection of pre-trained models to facilitate further research.

Concurrently, external encyclopedias like Wikipedia are frequently employed as valuable supplementary sources. promising artificial neural network algorithms for handling sequential data, including natural language, audio, and time series. Unlike conventional feed-forward networks, recurrent networks possess an inherent feedback loop that enables the storage of temporal context and the propagation of state information across entire event sequences. This capability facilitates state-of-the-art performance in critical tasks such as language modeling, stock market forecasting, image captioning, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. Nevertheless, training feed-forward networks typically demands extensive computational resources and significant human-annotated datasets. In contrast, training unsupervised feedback systems like unsupervised state machines is generally more efficient, requiring less manual labeling. Although system-level feedback has historically been difficult to implement due to safety and stability concerns, the emergence of neural feedback systems over the past decade has removed many of these barriers. This survey offers a comprehensive overview of various unsupervised feedback systems, spanning feedback neurons, neuroevolution, energy-based models, trajectory optimization, and probabilistic inference. By examining the principles, pros and cons, and applications of each category, we aim to inspire future research into feedback-like neural systems for state estimation, memory, and computation. The presented survey, alongside an accompanying library, serves as a foundational resource for advancing feedback-like neural system design. We anticipate that systems incorporating feedback will become increasingly vital in the future due to their superior efficiency, memory capacity, and computational capabilities compared to feed-forward architectures. The central concept uniting these fields is a linear space of matrices. We will demonstrate that multiple key definitions arising from these disciplines can be formulated as properties of such a space, with significant implications for enumerative algebraic geometry. The unifying combinatorial foundation for these definitions is a family of partitions of a positive integer $d$. Each partition gives rise to a specific arrangement of codimulations within the product of dual positive orthants of simplexes. This structure serves as a non-trivial example of a matrix linear space, a fact we establish through algebraic and poset-based combinatorial methods. The study of partitions and codimulations is inherently enumerated by Lorentzian polynomials. This family structure is inherently enumerated by a generalized class of Lorentzian polynomials, also known as segmented or stratified Lorentzian polynomials. experimental investigation into the pressure-induced transition from hexagonal close-packed (hcp) to body-centered cubic (bcc) in sodium placed within a carbon nanotube. Our findings indicate that the pressure threshold for this hcp-to-bcc transformation is significantly lowered by the presence of the nanotube. We further explore how the diameter of the nanotube influences the stability of the hcp structure and establish a clear relationship between the tube size and the hcp-to-bcc transition pressure. Specifically, our results demonstrate that the hcp phase is stabilized at zero pressure for sodium atoms confined in a carbon nanotube with a radius of 0.52 nm, corresponding to a (4,2) configuration. This finding is highlighted by an imaginary phonon frequency associated with certain modes. Additionally, analysis of the electron density of states and its momentum distribution reveals that the Hückel electrons follow Fermi-Dirac statistics, exhibiting a three-dimensional parabolic distribution characteristic of a metal. The ease with which an electron can occupy a higher energy state is effectively controlled by the confinement imposed by the carbon nanotube. Through this mechanism, the hcp-to-bcc transition is readily achieved through pressure application, even though the system remains in a metallic state. Finally, we examine how the pressure-driven shift from hcp to bcc alters the total binding and cohesive energies, finding that the binding energy increases by up to 35% while the cohesive energy rises by 12% following the transition. These observations underscore the significance of quantum size effects on the equation of state in nanostructured materials. We believe these results offer valuable insights for future research on quantum-confined metals.

Question: Does the hcp phase remain stable at zero pressure for sodium within a (4,2) carbon nanotube? Answer: Yes.

Question: Does the system remain in a metallic state after the hcp-to-bcc transition? Answer: Yes.

Question: Which factor controls the total binding and cohesive energies following the hcp-to-bcc transition? Answer: The bcc phase.

while high-order statistics of graphs offer superior descriptive power for real-world applications, standard graph analytics tools fail to support the high-scale computation of these data. To bridge this data analytic gap, we introduce a novel framework designed for high-order graph statistics computation. This framework accelerates computation across various workload patterns by adapting to query characteristics, while also providing a mechanism to discover and infer reusable data access patterns for further query acceleration. Furthermore, we develop an execution plan generator that guarantees sub-linear query execution time relative to the number of high-degree nodes. Comprehensive evaluations using both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that our framework achieves up to 2.36-core acceleration for two pattern selection strategies and up to 5.76-core acceleration for two pattern inference strategies compared to state-of-the-art methods. RingPop, a large-scale high-degree node database, serves as a leading state-of-the-art approach for baseline comparisons. Additionally, across 11 cases with varying degrees of framework configuration, a 2-to-three order of magnitude reduction in query execution time is achieved relative to generic query processors, validating the framework's 2.5-core average acceleration capability. We also detail the process of workloads derived from social apps, which constitutes a significant portion of the extensive benchmark suite. This contributes to the field by establishing a comprehensive benchmark dataset for emerging analytics on graph data. Across 21 cases, our findings validate the necessity of both a unified query representation and a unified engine for graph data. Furthermore, our results highlight the significant performance gains achievable through the proposed framework's adaptations to query data access patterns, particularly given the constrained resource environment of high-degree nodes. We examine the problem of learning a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from data, focusing on scenarios where the DAG structure is known in advance, though the associated variable potentials and conditional dependencies remain unknown. We outline a strategy to employ convex relaxation for estimating these hidden parameters, demonstrating that this method is always convex when the prior structure is present. We analyze the statistical properties of the resulting estimator, proving almost sure convergence as samples approach infinity and providing finite-sample error bounds under specific conditions. Our statistical findings are supported by experiments on extensive datasets, encompassing real-world cases where the prior structure is given.

Utilizing the standard Boussinesq approximation for buoyancy-driven natural convection, we disregard the effects of turbulent diffusivity eddy coefficients. The resulting model for vertical velocity perturbations, which accounts for both vertical and horizontal viscosity, yields a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein (TG) differential equation. To achieve this, the authors developed a new mathematical algorithm capable of detecting defects within discrete data representing potential periodic patterns. The method involves constructing a pattern-based discrete Gaussian noise model. Models are generated using discrete data from either defect-free or defect-containing patterns, where discrete points are sourced from Fourier samples of the data. These existing techniques, such as current-differential relays and component-injection schemes, rely on physical conservation laws to detect faults. However, these laws no longer apply to cyber-physical anomalies, which include attacks on sensing, actuating, and communication systems. To address this, the study introduces a data-driven differential relation mining method and a corresponding detection scheme for such attacks. Specifically, a new class of differential equations is derived from three-phase systems or pairs of phases. This equation serves as both a control feedback mechanism and an anomaly detector. During normal operations, the system maintains a steady state where the detector output remains zero; any deviation indicates a potential attack. Additionally, each equation functions as a soft constraint within the optimal control problem, enabling state estimation alongside optimization. Finally, a specific malicious DC-bias attack is designed to trap the detection scheme within a Zeno state. The proposed detection scheme requires no communication between devices, while the attack can be executed without direct access to the ESS control software. Simulation outcomes from a test power distribution system demonstrate the effectiveness of both the attack and the corresponding detection strategy. Furthermore, the study establishes performance metrics—including precision, recall, and response time—for both the attack and the detection scheme.

The rapid expansion of power distribution networks (PDN) into complex grids, characterized by two-way power flows, advanced automation, and extensive sensor and communication infrastructure, has exposed significant vulnerabilities to cyber-physical attacks. These malicious activities can disrupt power supply and degrade performance for consumers. While existing open-source simulation environments like OPF-GEN have facilitated the development of various attack scenarios, they often overlook the underlying optimization principles of PDN operations. This paper enhances attack design capabilities by deriving a comprehensive set of open-source optimization equations that accurately model normal PDN operations. Furthermore, it proposes two generalized attack strategies: one that disrupts the optimization equations and another that targets communication channels conveying optimization parameters. To evaluate the detectability of these attacks, the study also presents a coordinated detection scheme integrating state estimation with optimization. This framework establishes a performance benchmark for attack detection and communicates the inherent trade-offs between operational performance and security. Finally, the paper establishes a baseline for both attack execution and defense using open-source simulation environments, encouraging further research into more effective countermeasures. The developed equations are compiled into an open-source repository to support future attacks and defensive strategies. This collection fills a critical gap in simulation resources and accelerates research into new protective schemes for smart distribution networks. Numer

Federated Learning (FL) addresses this by training DCNNs across distributed, private datasets without exchanging raw images, thereby overcoming data centralization issues. In contrast, Transfer Learning (TL) improves model robustness and reduces training requirements through knowledge transfer, though it necessitates access to a substantial private training image set. This paper introduces a novel privacy-enhanced training framework that integrates DCNNs, TL, and FL, enabling robust recognition from completely private datasets. Furthermore, we develop a new FL strategy named Range Reports (RRFLTLDCNN), designed for federated range recognition. RRFLTLDCNN facilitates DCNN training on unaligned, private datasets of varying sizes via feature transfer, eliminates the need to share raw images, and avoids data aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate that RRFLTLDCNN achieves superior recognition accuracy compared to standard FL and TL DCNNs while demanding smaller training image sets. To validate these benefits, we conducted experiments using MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets. We also propose scoring metrics to assess the impact of model transfer and RRFLTLDCNN's robustness on recognition accuracy across different training sets. These metrics reveal that RRFLTLDCNN outperforms standard FL and TL DCNNs in terms of both range recognition accuracy and data privacy. The source code is accessible at the provided link.

This study develops a theoretical framework grounded in axisymmetric Stokes equations to investigate how liquid-solid slip affects the Rayleigh-Plateau instability of cylindrical films on fibers. The proposed model reveals that the classical Casson-Bennett prediction of complete stability is only achieved when slip is absent. When slip is present, the revolution geometry of the fiber significantly influences filamentary droplet formation and drops running down the fiber. Specifically, increasing the slip length results in a lower critical radius-to-outer-diameter ratio and a reduced dimensionless film thickness, enabling axial instabilities. Droplets travel down the fiber at high speeds with a shape approximating an oscillating Newtonian catenary and a small Newtonian head at the trailing edge. A theoretical expression for the drop speed is derived by applying boundary layers to matching Newtonian and non-Newtonian (Casson) regions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the number of droplets generated is finite. Drop spacing is primarily determined by the fiber's length and slightly by the spooling radius. The theoretical predictions align well with experimental findings from the boundary-selective coating of a fiber using a magnetic ferroliquid. Additionally, the impact of slip and magnetic fields on long-string instabilities is examined. As the slip length grows, the critical radius-to-outer-diameter ratio required to trigger rolling drops decreases, while the critical radius for long-string instabilities increases. Furthermore, the magnetic field suppresses long-string instabilities and causes running drops to become more symmetric and elongated toward the front as the magnetic body force increases. Finally, a comparative analysis between slipping and non-slipping long films is provided.

However, the remaining 21 of their questions remain open and could potentially be addressed in future research.

2021 "Puzzle Box" challenge, which involves traversing a grid by interpreting a sequence of directional instructions encoded in a 2D magnetic field. We developed a general algorithm to resolve this problem, demonstrating its efficacy across three difficulty levels. The method successfully predicts the outcome of a character navigating a specific path, allowing for an inverse application where a desired destination determines the necessary trajectory. The core mechanism relies on the conservative nature of the magnetic field, which ensures the existence of a scalar potential function capable of describing system dynamics and facilitating easy computation of both trajectory and final position. We detail an algorithm to construct this potential from the magnetic field and a trace, along with two additional algorithms to predict final positions for trajectories confined to contours of constant potential or to points directly, respectively. To address scenarios involving large state spaces, we also address strategies for systematically exploring these spaces to locate an optimal trajectory. Our approach was employed in the competition to determine directions leading to the lowest potential containing the target point. This work was created for the contest, and while it demonstrates how to solve the specific instance presented, it may not always be the most efficient solution for all possible targets. Furthermore, the problem's association with conservative vector fields connects it to other domains, including several video games. "Puzzle Box" was designed by Microsoft to highlight how concepts from mathematics and physics can aid in solving navigation problems within robotic and virtual contexts. Specifically, the problem illustrates a scenario where an object moves through a region experiencing a 2D force represented as a 2D magnetic field. Finally, we examine how this approach extends to other situations, such as enabling simultaneous achievement of multiple objectives, including optimal trajectory and energy consumption. The primary disadvantage of the solution is its inability to directly identify the shortest path in many instances; however, this can be overcome by employing strategies like evaluating all feasible paths using the scalar field to assess their quality. Our source code, C++ programs, and problem statements are accessible at https://www.puzzle-box.com.

(PAE) designed to separate cosmic foregrounds from the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Our approach treats each foreground map as a combination of large-scale dust and intermediate-scale dust, both modeled as modified blackbodies characterized by emission temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$) and opacity frequency dependence ($\beta_{\rm eff}$). The effective opacity frequency is either constrained to a single value for all data or allowed to vary independently for each channel. By applying a CMB template from the Planck 2018 Low-L multipole range ($\ell<30$), we isolate the remaining map as the CMB in four frequencies and locate the foreground component with the highest amplitude in the long-wavelength sector. Testing on both synthetic and real data, our method achieves optimal cross-spectral variance reduction (XSR) between model and data projections onto the CMB template l-space, improving by 18% over the data-driven Probabilistic Factor Analysis (PFA) method across all sectors. While PAE shows marginal gains in extracting modified blackbody parameters compared to PFA, it effectively decomposes the data into model components with greater physical interpretability. Consequently, our results indicate that PAE serves as a superior method for CMB foreground removal. However, achieving even lower XSR values requires either extending the temperature range used for the CMB template or incorporating a sparsity prior on the probability distributions of temperature and opacity. These enhancements will be explored in a forthcoming paper. In contrast, we propose that reshaping the network topology is a more effective strategy. Specifically, we demonstrate that shifting individual contacts from hub nodes to peripheral leaves—thereby creating shorter interaction chains—can significantly reduce the basic reproduction number, $R_0$. This topological transformation, known as topotherapy, encompasses both physical and informational disease spread and serves as a complementary approach to vaccination. Our findings indicate that topotherapy is most impactful when targeting hub nodes with a high intrinsic transmission probability, whereas strategies focusing on leaves are superior when hubs exhibit a low transmission rate. Topotherapeutic interventions achieve their maximum efficiency when they increase the total number of interactions. Furthermore, we show that combining topotherapy with vaccination yields an even more profound reduction in $R_0$. The model's applicability extends to various scenarios involving network topology changes, including the propagation of misinformation, financial scams, and terrorist attacks. Topotherapy offers a cost-effective alternative to vaccination, potentially eliminating the need to isolate hazardous environments. Ultimately, we contend that a comprehensive understanding of network topology is essential for formulating an optimal strategy to prevent disease outbreaks.

the correctness of communication protocols, which serve as the foundation for many critical applications. For complex systems, the state space can become so vast that exhaustive exploration is unfeasible without optimized techniques. One such technique is state space exploration guided by a predicate of interest, which reduces the explored state space to only those states satisfying that predicate. However, this method has a significant constraint: it can only handle existential queries, returning "yes" or "no" based on the presence of a satisfying state, rather than functional queries designed to extract specific information. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a stream exploration strategy that utilizes symbolic exploration for existence checks while concurrently executing the system of interest to retrieve maximal relevant information associated with the predicate. This approach not only facilitates system verification but also enables the systematic gathering of maximal data required for answering functional queries, effectively avoiding the traditionally expensive search phase. The proposed method is evaluated on two application examples, with one showing an exponential improvement compared to symbolic exploration-based solutions. Ultimately, this work marks the first attempt at integrating state space exploration with functional querying, marking a new phase in model checking. By focusing on maximal search, the technique is inherently applicable to a broad range of questions. Furthermore, the approach is general enough to explore unique states while gathering maximal valuable information, thereby eliminating the need for repetitive verification runs when multiple related questions are posed. This represents a fundamental shift from return-based answer generation to stream-based information flow, which also aids in keeping the explored state space manageable. By gathering maximal information during the exploration phase, the technique renders subsequent query phases nearly cost-free, dramatically lowering the complexity of answering functional queries even when they involve rare events. Consequently, this enables the answering of functional queries that were previously too complex to perform, opening up a new era in model checking. A key advantage of proposed methods must be demonstrated through comparison with the state of the art; therefore, our approach is evaluated against two existing solutions from current literature. Keywords: Model Checking, Communication Protocols, Functional Queries, Stream Explorations, Maximal Search.
